subtopics.title: Microprocessor Basics & Architecture
subtopics.subtitle: What a microprocessor is, buses, the instruction cycle, generations and a map of 2.4

concepts.text: What a Microprocessor Is

A microprocessor is a programmable, clock-driven, register-based semiconductor device that reads binary instructions from memory, processes data according to those instructions and delivers results to memory or output devices. It is the central processing unit (CPU) of a computer fabricated on a single chip. On its own it can do nothing: it needs external memory to hold the program and data, and I/O devices to communicate with the outside world. Intel's 8085 and 8086 are the two processors the NEC syllabus is built around.
Microprocessor vs microcontroller, and the basic job of every processor:
items: Microprocessor: only the CPU on the chip (8085, 8086, Pentium). Memory, timers and I/O ports are separate chips connected over the system bus; suited to general-purpose computers.
Microcontroller: CPU, ROM/RAM, timers and I/O ports integrated on one chip (8051, PIC, AVR); suited to embedded control where cost, size and power matter.
Whatever the family, the processor repeats one loop endlessly: fetch an instruction from memory, decode it, execute it, and store the result.

concepts.text: Buses and Timing
Three groups of lines connect the microprocessor to memory and I/O (the system bus):
items: Address bus: unidirectional, driven by the processor. With n lines it can select 2^n distinct locations: 16 lines (8085) reach 64 KB, 20 lines (8086) reach 1 MB.
Data bus: bidirectional; its width is the word size of the processor and fixes how many bits move per transfer (8 for 8085, 16 for 8086).
Control bus: individual signals that time and qualify transfers, e.g. RD, WR, IO/M, ALE, READY, interrupt request and acknowledge, HOLD/HLDA.

concepts.plainText: N = 2^n locations, where n = number of address lines

concepts.text: Timing is built from the clock. One T-state is one period of the processor clock. A machine cycle is the time taken for one complete bus operation (opcode fetch, memory read, memory write, I/O read, I/O write or interrupt acknowledge) and takes 3 to 6 T-states. An instruction cycle is the time to fetch and execute one whole instruction and consists of 1 to 5 machine cycles; on the 8085 this ranges from 4 T-states (MOV A, B) to 18 T-states (CALL). The first machine cycle of every instruction is always an opcode fetch.
Internal blocks common to all microprocessors:
items: Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU): performs add, subtract, AND, OR, XOR, compare, shift and rotate on data supplied by the registers; its result updates the flag register.
Register array: fast on-chip storage for operands, addresses and status (accumulator, general-purpose registers, program counter, stack pointer, flags).
Control unit: decodes the opcode and generates the timing and control signals that steer data over the internal bus and out to the system bus.

Clock: from a crystal; the 8085 internally halves its 6.144 MHz crystal to 3.072 MHz, so one T-state is about 325 ns. Speed is quoted as clock frequency or as MIPS = clock / (average clocks per instruction × 10^6).

rows: Von Neumann: one memory and one bus shared by program and data; simpler but the shared bus is a bottleneck
Harvard: separate program and data memories with separate buses; instruction and data fetch can overlap
RISC: few simple fixed-length instructions, one per clock, load/store only touches memory, many registers, hardwired control
CISC: many complex variable-length instructions, memory operands allowed, fewer registers, microprogrammed control

concepts.text: Roadmap of section 2.4, in the order the app presents it:
items: Intel 8085 architecture: registers, flags, pins, interrupts and instruction length.
Intel 8086 architecture: BIU/EU pipelining, segment and general registers, 9 flags, min/max mode, memory banks.
Segment:offset and physical address calculation: physical = segment × 10H + offset with worked examples.
Addressing modes of 8085 and 8086: how an instruction says where its operand is.
Instruction set and assembly language programming: instruction groups, directives, a worked program, stack and procedures.

concepts.text: MCQs on this section are mostly one-line factual recall (bus widths, memory capacity, register names, flag bits, vector addresses) plus short calculations: 2^n memory size, T-state duration from a clock frequency, and 8086 physical addresses. Learn the standard numbers exactly; distractors are usually the same numbers shifted by one power of two or one hex digit.
Going Deeper: Memory Sizing, Instruction Timing and Performance

Why do n address lines give exactly 2^n locations? Each line carries one bit, so the address is an n-bit binary number, and an n-bit number has 2^n distinct patterns from all zeros to all ones. The first address is therefore 0 and the last is 2^n − 1, which in hex is simply n/4 digits of F when n is a multiple of 4 (16 lines → FFFFH, 20 lines → FFFFFH). If each location holds a word wider than one byte, the capacity in bytes is the number of locations multiplied by the word width in bytes.

concepts.plainText: Capacity in bytes = 2^n × w/8 (w = bits per location); last address = 2^n − 1

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: memory sizing
Given: 20 address lines, each location 16 bits wide
Locations      = 2^20 = 1,048,576 = 1 M
Bytes/location = 16 / 8 = 2
Capacity       = 1 M x 2 = 2 MB
Address range  = 00000H to FFFFFH (2^20 - 1)
Reverse: lines needed for 256 KB bytes
256 KB = 2^8 x 2^10 = 2^18  ->  18 address lines

The fetch–decode–execute loop can be written as a short sequence of register transfers. The program counter drives the address bus, memory returns the opcode on the data bus into the instruction register, and the PC is incremented so it already points to the next byte. The decoder then decides how many more machine cycles are needed: none for a register-to-register operation, one or two memory reads to collect an operand or address, and a memory or I/O write if a result must leave the chip.

Instruction cycle as register transfers
FETCH:   address bus <- PC
         IR <- memory[PC]        (read strobe active)
         PC <- PC + 1
DECODE:  control unit examines IR, plans remaining cycles
OPERAND: (if needed) read further bytes, PC <- PC + 1 each
EXECUTE: ALU operates, flags updated
STORE:   (if needed) memory or I/O write of the result

concepts.plainText: CPU time = instruction count × CPI / f_clk; average CPI = sum of (fraction × CPI) over instruction classes

concepts.text:
Worked example 2: timing and performance
Clock 2 MHz  ->  T = 1 / 2 MHz = 0.5 us
Program: 20 instr x 4T + 10 x 7T + 5 x 10T
Total T-states = 80 + 70 + 50 = 200
Time = 200 x 0.5 us = 100 us
Mix: 50% CPI 1, 30% CPI 3, 20% CPI 2 at 900 MHz
CPI_avg = 0.5 + 0.9 + 0.4 = 1.8
MIPS = 900 / 1.8 = 500

rows: (f / clocks per bus cycle) × bytes per transfer

concepts.text: Special cases and common mistakes:
items: The 8085 clock generator divides the crystal by 2, so always halve the crystal frequency before computing T; the 8086 with an 8284 clock generator divides by 3.
4000H is the number of locations for 14 lines, not the last address; the last address is 3FFFH.
A wider data bus moves more bits per transfer but does not add any addressable locations.
Pipelining reduces the average time per instruction, not the time of a single instruction; the first instruction still needs all k stages.

concepts.text: When a memory is word-addressable, 2^n gives words, not bytes. Multiply by the word width in bytes before quoting KB or MB, and keep bits (Kbit) and bytes (KB) apart.

For timing problems write three lines every time: T = 1/f, total T-states = sum over instructions, time = total × T. For performance problems, find the average CPI first, then MIPS = f in MHz divided by CPI.

formulas.plainText: Memory capacity = 2^n × word size (n address lines)
Instruction cycle = sum of its machine cycles (1 to 5 on the 8085)
MIPS = f_clk / (CPI × 10^6), CPI = average clocks per instruction

notes.text: Address lines fix memory size, data lines fix word size. 16 lines → 64 KB, 20 lines → 1 MB, 24 lines → 16 MB, 32 lines → 4 GB. Every extra address line doubles the capacity.

Do not confuse the three timing units: T-state (one clock period) < machine cycle (one bus operation, 3–6 T-states) < instruction cycle (1–5 machine cycles). The opcode fetch is always the first machine cycle.
The 8085 and 8086 are Von Neumann, CISC processors. RISC (ARM, MIPS) and Harvard (8051, DSPs) appear only as comparison points in this syllabus.

formulas.title: Addressable locations
formulas.plainText: N = 2^n locations for n address lines
formulas.description: The number of memory locations a processor can select directly; 8085 (n = 16) gives 64 KB, 8086 (n = 20) gives 1 MB.

formulas.title: T-state duration
formulas.description: One T-state is one clock period; at 3 MHz it is 333 ns, at 5 MHz it is 200 ns.

formulas.title: Instruction time
formulas.plainText: Instruction time = total T-states × T-state duration
formulas.description: Multiply the T-state count of an instruction (4 to 18 on the 8085) by the clock period to get its execution time.

formulas.title: MIPS rating
formulas.description: Millions of instructions per second from the clock frequency and the average number of clocks per instruction.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a microprocessor and a microcontroller?
flashcards.back: A microprocessor is only the CPU on a chip (8085, 8086) and needs external memory and I/O; a microcontroller integrates CPU, memory, timers and I/O ports on one chip (8051, PIC).

flashcards.front: Define T-state, machine cycle and instruction cycle.
flashcards.back: T-state: one clock period. Machine cycle: one complete bus operation such as opcode fetch or memory read (3–6 T-states). Instruction cycle: fetch plus execute of one instruction (1–5 machine cycles).

flashcards.front: How does Harvard architecture differ from Von Neumann?
flashcards.back: Harvard keeps program and data in separate memories with separate buses so instruction and data access can overlap; Von Neumann shares one memory and one bus for both (8085, 8086).

flashcards.front: Give three features of RISC compared with CISC.
flashcards.back: RISC: few simple fixed-length instructions executing in about one clock, only LOAD/STORE touch memory, many registers and hardwired control. CISC (x86): many complex variable-length instructions, memory operands and microprogrammed control.

questions.questionText: A microprocessor with a 24-bit address bus and an 8-bit data bus can directly address a maximum memory of:
questions.explanation: Capacity = 2^24 locations = 16,777,216 bytes = 16 MB. The data bus width does not change the number of addressable locations.

questions.questionText: An 8085 operates from a 3 MHz internal clock. The duration of one T-state is approximately:
questions.explanation: One T-state is one clock period: T = 1 / (3 × 10^6) = 333 ns. An opcode fetch of 4 T-states therefore takes about 1.33 μs.

questions.questionText: A Harvard architecture processor differs from a Von Neumann processor in that it:
options: uses a single memory for program and data
has no need for a control unit
keeps program and data in separate memories with separate buses
questions.explanation: Harvard architecture provides separate program and data memories and buses so instruction fetch and data access can overlap; Von Neumann machines such as the 8085 share one memory and bus for both.

questions.questionText: Which block of a microprocessor decodes the opcode and generates the timing and control signals for the rest of the chip?
questions.explanation: The control unit interprets the fetched opcode and produces the sequence of internal and external control signals; the ALU only performs the arithmetic and logic operations it is told to perform.

questions.questionText: A byte-addressable microprocessor has 18 address lines. The maximum memory it can address directly is:
questions.explanation: Locations = 2^18 = 262,144 bytes = 256 KB. Each extra address line doubles the capacity, so 17 lines would give 128 KB and 19 lines 512 KB.

questions.questionText: How many address lines are needed to address 512 KB of byte-addressable memory directly?
questions.explanation: 512 KB = 2^9 × 2^10 = 2^19 bytes, so n = log2(2^19) = 19 address lines.

questions.questionText: A processor has 14 address lines A0–A13. The highest memory address it can generate is:
questions.explanation: Addresses run from 0 to 2^14 − 1 = 16383 = 3FFFH. 4000H (= 2^14) is the number of locations, not the last address.

questions.questionText: A memory is organised as 16-bit words and has 22 address lines, each address selecting one word. Its total capacity in bytes is:
questions.explanation: Words = 2^22 = 4 M words; each word is 2 bytes, so capacity = 4 M × 2 = 8 MB. Stopping at 2^22 gives 4 MB, which forgets the word size.

questions.questionText: A processor has 16 address lines, but in a particular board design A15 is permanently tied to 0 and A14 is used only to select I/O ports (memory is selected when A14 = 0). The maximum memory the board can use is:
questions.explanation: Only A13–A0 remain free to address memory, so memory = 2^14 = 16,384 bytes = 16 KB. Losing only A15 would leave 32 KB.

questions.questionText: A memory chip is specified as 4096 × 8. How many address and data lines does it need?
questions.explanation: 4096 = 2^12 locations need 12 address lines; each location is 8 bits wide, so 8 data lines.

questions.questionText: A 64 KB memory space is divided into equal blocks of 8 KB each. How many blocks are there, and how many of the 16 address lines select the block?
questions.explanation: Blocks = 64 KB / 8 KB = 8 = 2^3, so the top 3 address lines (A15–A13) select the block and the remaining 13 lines (A12–A0) address a byte inside it.

questions.questionText: A 4 KB ROM is placed in a memory map starting at address 8000H. Its address range is:
questions.explanation: 4 KB = 4096 = 1000H locations, so the last address = 8000H + 1000H − 1 = 8FFFH. 83FFH would be only 1 KB and BFFFH 16 KB.

questions.questionText: A processor with a 16-bit data bus must read a 1 KB block of memory. If every bus transfer moves one full data-bus width, the number of transfers needed is:
questions.explanation: Each transfer moves 16 bits = 2 bytes, so transfers = 1024 / 2 = 512. 1024 assumes an 8-bit bus; 64 divides by 16 bits as if they were bytes.

questions.questionText: A 3-byte instruction is stored in memory starting at address 3000H. After the processor has fetched all of its bytes, the program counter points to:
questions.explanation: The instruction occupies 3000H, 3001H and 3002H, and the PC is incremented after every byte fetched, so it ends at 3000H + 3 = 3003H, the first byte of the next instruction.

questions.questionText: A Harvard-architecture microcontroller has a 12-bit program address bus and 16-bit wide instruction words. The size of its program memory is:
questions.explanation: Program memory = 2^12 words × 16 bits = 4096 × 2 bytes = 8192 bytes = 8 KB. 4 KB counts locations only; 64 KB confuses the 64 Kbit total with bytes.

questions.questionText: A processor runs at 5 MHz. An instruction that takes 7 T-states executes in:
questions.explanation: T = 1 / 5 MHz = 0.2 µs, so time = 7 × 0.2 µs = 1.4 µs.

questions.questionText: An 8085A-2 uses a 10 MHz crystal, which the on-chip clock generator divides by 2. An instruction of 10 T-states takes:
questions.explanation: Operating clock = 10 MHz / 2 = 5 MHz, so T = 0.2 µs and time = 10 × 0.2 µs = 2 µs. Using the crystal frequency directly gives the wrong answer of 1 µs.

questions.questionText: A program executes 20 instructions of 4 T-states, 10 of 7 T-states and 5 of 10 T-states on a processor clocked at 2 MHz. Its execution time is:
An instruction cycle consists of three machine cycles of 4, 3 and 3 T-states. At a clock frequency of 4 MHz the instruction takes:
questions.explanation: Total = 4 + 3 + 3 = 10 T-states; T = 1 / 4 MHz = 0.25 µs; time = 10 × 0.25 µs = 2.5 µs. 0.75 µs wrongly counts one T-state per machine cycle.

questions.questionText: What clock frequency gives a T-state of 250 ns?
A processor has a clock period of 0.5 µs. How many T-states are needed to produce a software delay of exactly 1 ms?
questions.explanation: Number of T-states = delay / T = 1 ms / 0.5 µs = 1000 µs / 0.5 µs = 2000.

questions.questionText: A processor runs at 200 MHz with an average of 4 clock cycles per instruction (CPI). Its MIPS rating is:
An 8-bit processor runs at 3 MHz and its instructions take 5 T-states on average. Its speed in MIPS is:
questions.explanation: MIPS = f / (CPI × 10^6) = 3 × 10^6 / (5 × 10^6) = 0.6. 15 multiplies instead of dividing.

questions.questionText: A program of 2 × 10^6 instructions runs on a 500 MHz processor with an average CPI of 2.5. The CPU execution time is:
questions.explanation: CPU time = instruction count × CPI / f = 2 × 10^6 × 2.5 / (500 × 10^6) = 0.01 s = 10 ms. Ignoring CPI gives 4 ms; dividing by CPI gives 1.6 ms.

questions.questionText: A program mix is 50% ALU instructions (CPI 1), 30% load/store (CPI 3) and 20% branches (CPI 2). On a 900 MHz processor the MIPS rating is:
questions.explanation: Average CPI = 0.5×1 + 0.3×3 + 0.2×2 = 0.5 + 0.9 + 0.4 = 1.8. MIPS = 900 / 1.8 = 500. 1620 multiplies by CPI; 450 uses a CPI of 2.

questions.questionText: A system bus is 16 bits wide and one bus cycle takes 4 clock periods at 8 MHz. The maximum data transfer rate is:
questions.explanation: Bus cycles per second = 8 × 10^6 / 4 = 2 × 10^6; each moves 2 bytes, so rate = 2 × 10^6 × 2 = 4 × 10^6 bytes/s = 4 MB/s (decimal megabytes). Forgetting the 2 bytes gives 2 MB/s.

questions.questionText: An ideal 5-stage instruction pipeline (one clock per stage, no stalls) executes 100 instructions. The number of clock cycles required is:
questions.explanation: Cycles = k + (n − 1) = 5 + 99 = 104: the first instruction needs 5 cycles to fill the pipeline, then one instruction completes every cycle. 500 is the unpipelined count.

questions.questionText: Which of the following devices integrates a CPU, RAM, ROM, timers and I/O ports on a single chip?
questions.explanation: The 8051 is a microcontroller with on-chip memory, timers, serial port and I/O ports. The 8085, 8086 and 80386 are microprocessors that need external memory and I/O chips.

questions.questionText: Which statement about microprocessors and microcontrollers is NOT correct?
options: A microprocessor needs external memory and I/O chips to form a working system
A microcontroller has on-chip memory, timers and I/O ports
A microcontroller is preferred for general-purpose personal computers because of its large external memory
Microcontrollers are preferred in embedded products where cost, size and power matter
questions.explanation: General-purpose computers use microprocessors with large external memory; microcontrollers are built for dedicated embedded control with limited on-chip memory.

questions.questionText: Which bus of a microprocessor system is bidirectional?
questions.explanation: The data bus carries data from memory/I/O to the processor during a read and from the processor to them during a write, so it is bidirectional. The address bus is driven only by the processor.

questions.questionText: Why is the address bus of a simple microprocessor system called unidirectional?
options: It carries data in one direction during reads and the other during writes
Only the processor places addresses on it; memory and I/O only receive them
It can address only one memory chip at a time
It is used only for the instruction fetch operation
questions.explanation: The processor alone generates the address of the memory location or port it wants; memory and I/O devices decode it but never drive it (DMA controllers aside, which take over the bus only after the processor releases it).

questions.questionText: The word length of a microprocessor refers to:
options: the number of bits it can process in one operation, set by its ALU and data-bus width
the number of address lines it provides
the number of instructions in its instruction set
the number of bytes in its longest instruction
questions.explanation: Word length is the size of the data the processor handles at once; an 8085 is an 8-bit processor even though it has 16 address lines.

questions.questionText: If a microprocessor's data bus is widened from 8 to 16 bits while its address bus stays at 16 bits, what changes?
options: The number of addressable locations doubles to 2^17
The number of addressable locations halves
Neither the transfer width nor the number of locations changes
The number of bits moved per bus transfer doubles; the number of addressable locations stays 2^16
questions.explanation: Address lines alone fix the number of locations (2^n); data lines fix how many bits move per transfer.

questions.questionText: In the fetch–decode–execute cycle, which step immediately follows fetching the opcode into the instruction register?
options: Decoding the opcode in the control unit
questions.explanation: After the opcode is fetched it must be decoded so the control unit knows which operation and which further machine cycles are required; execution comes after decoding.

questions.questionText: During the fetch phase of an instruction, which sequence of events is correct?
options: The PC is placed on the address bus, the opcode is read into the IR and the PC is incremented
The SP is placed on the address bus, the opcode is read into the accumulator and the SP is decremented
The IR is placed on the address bus, the opcode is read into the PC and the PC is decremented
The accumulator is placed on the address bus and the opcode is written to memory
questions.explanation: The program counter supplies the address of the next instruction, the memory returns the opcode on the data bus into the instruction register, and the PC is incremented to point to the next byte.

questions.questionText: Which register holds the opcode of the current instruction while it is being decoded?
questions.explanation: The fetched opcode is latched into the instruction register (IR), whose output feeds the instruction decoder. The PC already points to the next byte.

questions.questionText: The program counter of a microprocessor holds:
options: the address of the next instruction byte to be fetched
the opcode of the instruction being executed
the number of instructions executed since reset
the address of the top of the stack
questions.explanation: The PC is a 16-bit pointer (in the 8085) that always addresses the next byte of the program; it is incremented after each fetch and reloaded by jumps, calls and returns.

questions.questionText: What does the flag (status) register of a microprocessor record?
options: The address of the next instruction
The operand of the current instruction
Conditions of the result of the last arithmetic or logic operation, such as zero, sign and carry
questions.explanation: Flag bits are set or reset by the ALU to describe the result (zero, negative, carry, parity and so on); conditional jumps test them.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is NOT a function of the ALU?
options: Decoding the opcode of the fetched instruction
Shifting or rotating a data byte
questions.explanation: Opcode decoding is done by the instruction decoder in the control unit. The ALU performs arithmetic, logic, shift and rotate operations on data.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is NOT a control-bus signal of a microprocessor system?
questions.explanation: RD, WR and ALE are control/timing signals. AD7 is a multiplexed address/data line, part of the address and data buses.

questions.questionText: Why are bus lines driven through tri-state buffers in a microprocessor system?
options: To increase the clock frequency of the processor
To convert the data bus into an address bus
So that a device can electrically disconnect itself (high impedance) and let another device drive the shared bus
To store data when the power fails
questions.explanation: Tri-state outputs have 0, 1 and high-impedance states; only one device drives a shared line at a time while the others float, which also lets a DMA controller take over the bus.

questions.questionText: One T-state of a microprocessor is:
options: one period of the processor clock
the time for one complete bus operation
the time to fetch and execute one instruction
the time for one memory write
questions.explanation: A T-state is the basic timing unit, equal to one clock period (1/f). A machine cycle is one bus operation and an instruction cycle is the complete fetch and execute of one instruction.

questions.questionText: Which ordering of timing units, from shortest to longest, is correct?
questions.explanation: A machine cycle is made of several T-states, and an instruction cycle is made of one or more machine cycles.

questions.questionText: A machine cycle is best defined as:
options: one period of the system clock
the time needed to execute the longest instruction
the time required to complete one operation of accessing memory or an I/O device
questions.explanation: Each machine cycle (opcode fetch, memory read, memory write, I/O read, I/O write, interrupt acknowledge) is one bus operation lasting several T-states.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of a RISC processor?
options: Fixed-length instructions that are easy to pipeline
Many variable-length instructions with complex memory addressing modes
Only load and store instructions access memory
A large set of general-purpose registers
questions.explanation: Variable-length instructions with rich memory addressing modes are the hallmark of CISC designs such as the x86. RISC keeps instructions simple, fixed-length and register-to-register.

questions.questionText: The control unit of a typical CISC processor is implemented as ___, while a typical RISC processor uses ___.
questions.explanation: Complex, variable instructions are easier to implement as microcode sequences stored in a control ROM; simple RISC instructions are decoded by fast hardwired logic.

questions.questionText: Why are RISC processors particularly well suited to pipelining?
options: Their instructions are of uniform length and similar execution time, so each stage takes about one clock
They have fewer registers, so less data has to be saved
They allow memory operands in every instruction
They use microcode for every instruction
questions.explanation: Uniform, simple instructions let fetch, decode, execute and write-back be divided into equal stages; variable-length CISC instructions make stage timing irregular.

questions.questionText: The "von Neumann bottleneck" refers to:
options: the small number of registers in RISC processors
the delay caused by interrupt handling
the heat generated by high clock speeds
the limit on throughput because instructions and data share one memory and one bus
questions.explanation: In a von Neumann machine an instruction fetch and a data access cannot use the single bus at the same time, so the bus limits performance; Harvard architecture removes this by using separate buses.

questions.questionText: Which statement about von Neumann and Harvard architectures is correct?
options: The 8085 follows the Harvard model because it has separate RD and WR lines
A Harvard processor cannot store constant data in program memory in any form
Von Neumann processors always have separate instruction and data caches
The 8085 and 8086 follow the von Neumann model, whereas many DSPs and the 8051 follow the Harvard model
questions.explanation: The 8085/8086 fetch instructions and data from one memory over one bus. Separate RD and WR strobes do not make separate memories; DSPs and the 8051 have separate program and data spaces.

questions.questionText: The first commercial microprocessor, the Intel 4004, was a ___ processor.
questions.explanation: The 4004 (1971) had a 4-bit data path and a 12-bit address range; the 8008/8080/8085 were 8-bit and the 8086 16-bit.

subtopics.title: Intel 8085 Architecture
subtopics.subtitle: 8-bit CPU with 16-bit addressing: registers, flags, pins, interrupts, instruction length

concepts.text: Key Features of the 8085
The 8085 is Intel's classic 8-bit microprocessor (NMOS, 1976):
items: 8-bit data bus and 8-bit ALU; 16-bit address bus, so 2^16 = 64 KB of memory can be addressed directly.
40-pin DIP package, single +5 V supply, clock of about 3 MHz (a 6.144 MHz crystal is divided by 2 internally; the 8085A-2 runs at 5 MHz).
74 instructions (246 opcodes), 5 hardware interrupt pins, serial input/output on SID and SOD pins, on-chip clock generator and system controller.
Lower address byte is multiplexed with data on AD0–AD7 to save pins; ALE separates them.

concepts.text: Register Set

rows: One operand and the result of every ALU operation; source/destination for IN and OUT
B, C, D, E, H, L
General-purpose; usable as 16-bit pairs BC, DE, HL for addresses
Default memory pointer; the operand M means the byte at [HL]
Address of the top of stack; PUSH decrements by 2, POP increments by 2
Address of the next instruction byte to be fetched
Five status bits; A + F together form the program status word (PSW)
Internal only, not accessible to the programmer

concepts.text: Flag Register

rows: Bit 7 of the result is 1 (negative in 2's complement)
A carry passes from bit 3 to bit 4 (used by DAA for BCD)
The result has an even number of 1s
Carry out of bit 7 (or borrow in subtraction)

concepts.text: Bits D5, D3 and D1 are unused. Arithmetic and logic instructions update the flags; data transfer instructions (MOV, MVI, LDA, STA) never do. Only CY can be tested and changed directly (STC, CMC); the others are tested by conditional jumps and calls such as JZ, JNC, CP and CPE. PUSH PSW saves A and the flags together on the stack.
Pins and Signals
The 40 pins group into address, data, control, status, power and interrupt lines:
items: A8–A15: higher-order address, output only. AD0–AD7: lower-order address multiplexed with data.

ALE (Address Latch Enable): goes high during T1 of every machine cycle while AD0–AD7 carry the address; an external latch (74LS373) captures A0–A7 on its falling edge, after which the same lines carry data.
RD and WR (active low): read or write strobe for memory and I/O. IO/M: 1 selects an I/O port, 0 selects memory. S0 and S1: status of the current machine cycle (decoded in the table below).
READY: a slow device pulls it low to insert wait states. HOLD/HLDA: bus request and grant for DMA. RESET IN / RESET OUT, X1/X2 crystal, CLK OUT for the system, SID/SOD serial lines, +5 V and GND.

concepts.text: Interrupts

rows: Supplied by device (RST n or CALL)

concepts.text: Vectored interrupts jump to a fixed address equal to the interrupt number × 8 (RST 7.5 → 7.5 × 8 = 60 = 003CH). INTR has no fixed vector: the processor answers with INTA and reads an RST n or CALL opcode from the data bus. EI and DI enable or disable all maskable interrupts; SIM writes the individual masks for RST 7.5, 6.5 and 5.5 and drives the SOD pin, while RIM reads the mask status, pending interrupts and the SID pin. The SID/SOD pair gives the 8085 one-bit serial input and output without any extra chip.
Instruction Length
Every 8085 instruction is 1, 2 or 3 bytes long, decided by what the opcode needs to carry:
items: 1-byte: opcode only; operands are registers or implied. MOV A, B → 78H; ADD B → 80H; CMA → 2FH.
2-byte: opcode + one byte of 8-bit data or port address. MVI A, 32H → 3E 32; IN 05H → DB 05; ADI 10H → C6 10.
3-byte: opcode + 16-bit address or data stored low byte first (little-endian). LDA 2050H → 3A 50 20; LXI H, 2050H → 21 50 20; JMP 3000H → C3 00 30.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: 8085 Timing, Flags and the Stack

Every 8085 machine cycle begins the same way. In T1 the processor puts the high address byte on A8–A15, the low byte on AD0–AD7, sets IO/M, S1 and S0 to announce the kind of cycle, and pulses ALE so an external latch such as the 74LS373 holds A0–A7. In T2 the RD or WR strobe goes low and AD0–AD7 switch to data; READY is sampled here and wait states are inserted while it is low. T3 completes the transfer. An opcode fetch adds T4 to decode the opcode, and instructions that do 16-bit register work or pre-decrement SP (INX, DCX, SPHL, PCHL, PUSH, CALL, RST) stretch the fetch to 6 T-states.

rows: MOV r, r / ADD r / INR r
MOV r, M / MVI r / ADD M
MVI M / LXI / JMP / IN / OUT
OF, MR, MR, MR or MW
OF (6 T), MR, MR, MW, MW

concepts.text: Which instruction groups change which flags:
items: Arithmetic (ADD, ADI, ADC, SUB, SUI, SBB, CMP, CPI, DAA): all five flags; for subtraction and compare, CY = 1 means a borrow (A was smaller).
INR and DCR: S, Z, AC and P change, but CY is left untouched.
Logical AND (ANA, ANI): CY is reset and AC is set. OR and XOR (ORA, ORI, XRA, XRI): CY and AC are both reset. All three update S, Z and P.
Data transfer, INX, DCX, PUSH, POP (except POP PSW), jumps and calls: no flags change.

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: flags after ADI
A = 9AH, execute ADI 76H
   9AH = 1001 1010
 + 76H = 0111 0110
 = 1 0001 0000  -> A = 10H, carry out of bit 7 -> CY = 1
Low nibbles: A + 6 = 10H, carry from bit 3 -> AC = 1
A = 0001 0000: bit 7 = 0 -> S = 0; not zero -> Z = 0
One 1 in the result (odd) -> P = 0
Flag byte S Z 0 AC 0 P 0 CY = 0001 0001 = 11H

; Worked example 2: stack trace (8085)
        LXI SP, 2400H   ; SP = 2400H
        LXI B, 1234H    ; B = 12H, C = 34H
        PUSH B          ; [23FFH] = 12H, [23FEH] = 34H, SP = 23FEH
        CALL 4000H      ; at 2050H: push 2053H
                        ; [23FDH] = 20H, [23FCH] = 53H, SP = 23FCH
        ; ... subroutine ends with RET
        ; RET pops 53H then 20H: PC = 2053H, SP = 23FEH
        POP D           ; E = 34H, D = 12H, SP = 2400H

Software delays rely on knowing the exact T-states of a loop. In a loop that counts N times, the conditional jump is taken N − 1 times (10 T) and falls through once (7 T), so the last pass is 3 T shorter than the others. Adding the set-up instruction once gives a closed form, and multiplying by the clock period converts T-states to time.

Worked example 3: 8-bit delay loop at 2 MHz (T = 0.5 us)
        MVI C, 0AH     ; 7 T, once
LOOP:   DCR C          ; 4 T
        JNZ LOOP       ; 10 T taken, 7 T not taken
T_loop  = 4 + 10 = 14 T, N = 10
T_total = 7 + 9 x 14 + 11 = 144 T
Delay   = 144 x 0.5 us = 72 us

DCR does not set CY, so a loop counter that runs past 00H wraps to FFH silently. For a 16-bit counter use DCX followed by MOV A, C and ORA B, because DCX changes no flags at all and JNZ would otherwise test a stale Z flag.

For stack questions write the addresses down: PUSH or CALL stores the high byte at SP − 1 and the low byte at SP − 2, then SP = SP − 2. The return address of a CALL is the address after the 3-byte CALL, not the CALL itself. For PUSH PSW, build the flag byte as S Z 0 AC 0 P 0 CY.

formulas.plainText: Vector address of RST n = n × 8 (RST 7.5 → 60 = 003CH)
Instruction length = 1 opcode byte + 0, 1 or 2 operand bytes

notes.text: Memorise the flag bit positions S7 Z6 AC4 P2 CY0 and the vector table TRAP 0024H, RST 5.5 002CH, RST 6.5 0034H, RST 7.5 003CH. The vectors are 8 bytes apart, exactly like RST 0–7 (0000H, 0008H, ... 0038H).
RST 7.5 (hardware pin, vector 003CH) is not RST 7 (software instruction, vector 0038H). Likewise TRAP is the only non-maskable interrupt; INTR is the only one without a fixed vector.
Data transfer instructions never change flags. If an MCQ asks which flags MOV or STA affects, the answer is none.

formulas.title: 8085 address space
formulas.description: Sixteen address lines A0–A15 give the 8085 a 64 KB memory map from 0000H to FFFFH.

formulas.title: RST vector address
formulas.description: Restart instruction RST n and hardware pins RST 5.5/6.5/7.5 branch to n × 8: e.g. 6.5 × 8 = 52 = 0034H.

formulas.title: 8085 internal clock
formulas.description: The on-chip clock generator halves the crystal frequency; a 6.144 MHz crystal gives a 3.072 MHz operating clock.

formulas.title: Stack pointer after PUSH/POP
formulas.plainText: PUSH: SP = SP − 2; POP: SP = SP + 2
formulas.description: Each PUSH stores a register pair (two bytes) and moves the 16-bit stack pointer down; POP reverses it.

flashcards.front: List the five 8085 flags with their bit positions.
flashcards.back: S (bit 7), Z (bit 6), AC (bit 4), P (bit 2), CY (bit 0). Bits 5, 3 and 1 are unused.

flashcards.front: What does the ALE signal do in the 8085?
flashcards.back: Address Latch Enable pulses high in T1 while AD0–AD7 carry the low address byte; an external latch captures it so the same pins can then carry data. It demultiplexes the AD bus.

flashcards.front: Give the 8085 hardware interrupts in priority order with their vector addresses.
flashcards.back: TRAP (0024H, non-maskable) > RST 7.5 (003CH) > RST 6.5 (0034H) > RST 5.5 (002CH) > INTR (no fixed vector, device supplies RST n or CALL).

flashcards.front: How many bytes are MVI A, 32H and LDA 2050H, and how is 2050H stored?
flashcards.back: MVI A, 32H is 2 bytes (3E 32); LDA 2050H is 3 bytes stored little-endian as 3A 50 20, low byte first.

questions.questionText: The vector address of the RST 6.5 interrupt in the 8085 is:
questions.explanation: Vector = 6.5 × 8 = 52 = 0034H. RST 5.5 goes to 002CH, RST 7.5 to 003CH and TRAP to 0024H.

questions.questionText: Which 8085 signal is used to latch the lower-order address from the multiplexed AD0–AD7 lines?
questions.explanation: ALE (Address Latch Enable) goes high during T1 while AD0–AD7 hold address bits A0–A7; its falling edge clocks an external latch, after which the pins carry data.

questions.questionText: In the 8085, A = 9AH. After ADI 76H is executed, the accumulator and flags are:
questions.explanation: 9AH + 76H = 110H, so A = 10H with a carry out of bit 7 (CY = 1). Low nibbles A + 6 = 10H give a carry from bit 3 to bit 4 (AC = 1); the result is not zero, so Z = 0.

questions.questionText: In the 8085, CY = 0 and the instructions MVI A, FFH followed by INR A are executed. The result is:
questions.explanation: FFH + 1 wraps to 00H, so Z = 1. INR and DCR affect S, Z, AC and P but never CY, so CY keeps its previous value 0.

questions.questionText: In the 8085, B = 00H and CY = 1. After DCR B is executed:
questions.explanation: 00H − 1 wraps to FFH, whose bit 7 is 1, so S = 1. DCR does not touch CY, so the borrow is not recorded and CY stays 1.

questions.questionText: In the 8085, A = 35H and B = 4AH. After SUB B is executed, the contents of A and the S, CY and P flags are:
questions.explanation: 35H − 4AH = −15H, stored as the 2's complement EBH = 1110 1011. Bit 7 is 1 (S = 1), a borrow occurred (CY = 1), and six 1s is even parity (P = 1). 15H is B − A, the wrong way round.

questions.questionText: In the 8085, A = 40H and B = 60H. After CMP B is executed:
questions.explanation: CMP subtracts B from A internally only to set flags; A is unchanged. Since A < B a borrow occurs (CY = 1) and the operands differ (Z = 0).

questions.questionText: In the 8085, A = 5CH. After ANI 0FH is executed, A and the CY and AC flags are:
questions.explanation: 5CH AND 0FH = 0CH (the upper nibble is masked off). In the 8085 the AND instructions always reset CY and set AC; 5FH would be the OR result.

questions.questionText: In the 8085, A = 7BH and CY = 1. After XRA A is executed, the Z, P and CY flags are:
questions.explanation: Any value XOR itself is 00H, so Z = 1; 00H has zero 1s, which is even parity (P = 1); logical instructions reset CY. XRA A is a one-byte way to clear A and CY together.

questions.questionText: In the 8085, A = 7FH. After ADI 01H is executed, which flags are set (= 1)?
questions.explanation: 7FH + 01H = 80H = 1000 0000: bit 7 is 1 (S = 1), F + 1 carries from bit 3 to bit 4 (AC = 1), there is no carry out (CY = 0), and a single 1 is odd parity (P = 0).

questions.questionText: In the 8085, MVI A, 03H and then ADI 04H are executed. The resulting S, Z, P and CY flags are:
questions.explanation: A = 07H = 0000 0111. It is positive and non-zero, has three 1s (odd, so P = 0) and produces no carry.

questions.questionText: The 8085 flag register contains 45H. Which flags are set?
questions.explanation: 45H = 0100 0101: bit 6 (Z), bit 2 (P) and bit 0 (CY) are 1. The flag layout is S Z x AC x P x CY from D7 to D0.

questions.questionText: In the 8085, MVI A, 38H; ADI 45H; DAA are executed. The final content of A is:
questions.explanation: 38H + 45H = 7DH. The low nibble D is greater than 9, so DAA adds 06H: 7DH + 06H = 83H, the correct BCD sum of 38 + 45. The high nibble 8 needs no correction.

questions.questionText: In the 8085, SP = 2000H, A = 3CH and the flags are S = 1, Z = 0, AC = 1, P = 1, CY = 1 (unused bits 0). After PUSH PSW, the content of location 1FFEH and the new SP are:
questions.explanation: Flag byte = S Z 0 AC 0 P 0 CY = 1001 0101 = 95H. PUSH stores A at SP − 1 = 1FFFH and the flags at SP − 2 = 1FFEH, then SP = 1FFEH. D5H would wrongly include Z.

questions.questionText: In the 8085, SP = 2400H. After PUSH B and then PUSH D are executed, SP contains:
questions.explanation: Each PUSH stores two bytes and decrements SP by 2: 2400H − 2 − 2 = 23FCH. The stack grows towards lower addresses; 2396H comes from subtracting in decimal.

questions.questionText: In the 8085, B = 12H, C = 34H and SP = 3000H. After PUSH B is executed, the stack contains:
questions.explanation: PUSH decrements SP and stores the high register B at 2FFFH, decrements again and stores C at 2FFEH; SP ends at 2FFEH so the low byte is on top.

questions.questionText: In the 8085, the 3-byte instruction CALL 4000H is stored at 2050H and SP = 2400H. Immediately after the CALL executes:
questions.explanation: The return address is the next instruction, 2050H + 3 = 2053H. CALL pushes the high byte 20H at 23FFH and the low byte 53H at 23FEH, leaves SP = 23FEH and loads PC = 4000H.

questions.questionText: An 8085 fetches a complete 3-byte instruction whose first byte is at 20FEH. After all three bytes are fetched, the program counter contains:
questions.explanation: The bytes occupy 20FEH, 20FFH and 2100H, so the PC then points to 20FEH + 3 = 2101H. 2001H comes from losing the carry into the high byte.

questions.questionText: How many T-states does the 8085 instruction LDA 2050H take?
questions.explanation: LDA has four machine cycles: opcode fetch (4 T) + two memory reads for the address (3 + 3 T) + one memory read of the data (3 T) = 13 T-states. 16 T belongs to LHLD.

questions.questionText: An 8085 runs at 3 MHz. How long does IN 40H (opcode fetch, memory read, I/O read) take to execute?
questions.explanation: IN takes 4 + 3 + 3 = 10 T-states. T = 1 / 3 MHz = 0.333 µs, so time = 10 × 0.333 µs = 3.33 µs. 1 µs counts one T-state per machine cycle; 1.33 µs counts only the opcode fetch.

questions.questionText: An 8085 is driven by a 5 MHz crystal connected to X1 and X2. The duration of one T-state is:
questions.explanation: The internal clock is crystal / 2 = 2.5 MHz, so T = 1 / 2.5 MHz = 400 ns. Using 5 MHz directly gives 200 ns.

questions.questionText: An 8085 runs at 2 MHz. MOV A, M is executed from a slow memory that causes one wait state in the memory read cycle. The execution time is:
questions.explanation: Normally MOV A, M = 4 T (opcode fetch) + 3 T (memory read) = 7 T. One wait state adds 1 T, giving 8 T × 0.5 µs = 4 µs. 3.5 µs ignores the wait state.

questions.questionText: An 8085 at 2 MHz runs: MVI C, 0AH (7 T); LOOP: DCR C (4 T); JNZ LOOP (10 T if taken, 7 T if not). The total delay is:
questions.explanation: Total = 7 + (10 − 1) × (4 + 10) + (4 + 7) = 7 + 126 + 11 = 144 T. With T = 0.5 µs the delay is 144 × 0.5 = 72 µs. 144 µs uses 1 µs per T-state.

questions.questionText: An 8085 at 3 MHz runs: LXI B, 1000H (10 T); LOOP: DCX B (6 T); MOV A, C (4 T); ORA B (4 T); JNZ LOOP (10/7 T). The delay produced is approximately:
An 8085 at 2 MHz executes LXI H, 2050H; MOV A, M; INX H; ADD M; STA 2060H once. The total execution time is:
questions.explanation: T-states = 10 + 7 + 6 + 7 + 13 = 43 T. At 2 MHz, T = 0.5 µs, so time = 43 × 0.5 = 21.5 µs. 20.5 µs wrongly takes INX H as 4 T.

questions.questionText: How many machine cycles and T-states does the 8085 CALL instruction need?
questions.explanation: CALL = opcode fetch (6 T) + two memory reads for the address (3 + 3 T) + two memory writes to push the return address (3 + 3 T) = 5 cycles and 18 T.

questions.questionText: Which of the following 8085 registers is 16 bits wide?
questions.explanation: SP and PC are the 8085's only true 16-bit registers; A, H and the flag register are 8 bits (H and L can be combined into a 16-bit pair).

questions.questionText: Which 8085 registers are used internally by the processor and are NOT accessible to the programmer?
questions.explanation: The temporary register pair W–Z holds operand bytes during instructions such as CALL, JMP and LDA; no instruction can name them.

questions.questionText: In the 8085, the program status word (PSW) consists of:
options: the program counter and stack pointer
the accumulator and the flag register
the flag register and the instruction register
questions.explanation: PSW is the 16-bit unit formed by A (high byte) and the flags (low byte); PUSH PSW and POP PSW save and restore them together.

questions.questionText: Which 8085 instruction affects none of the flags?
questions.explanation: 16-bit increment and decrement (INX, DCX) change no flags. INR B affects S, Z, AC and P; CMP and ADD affect all five flags.

questions.questionText: In an 8085 machine cycle, the ALE signal is high during:
questions.explanation: ALE pulses high in the first T-state of every machine cycle, while AD0–AD7 carry A0–A7; the latch captures the address on its falling edge.

questions.questionText: Why does the 8085 multiplex the lower-order address with data on AD0–AD7?
options: To reduce the number of pins needed on the 40-pin package
To double the speed of memory access
To allow the 8085 to address 1 MB
To eliminate the need for a clock
questions.explanation: Sharing eight pins between A0–A7 and D0–D7 saves eight pins; the cost is an external latch and a little time in T1 to separate the two.

questions.questionText: Which chip is commonly used with the 8085 to latch the lower-order address byte from AD0–AD7?
questions.explanation: The 74LS373 is an 8-bit transparent latch whose enable is driven by ALE. The 74LS138 decodes addresses, the 74LS245 buffers the data bus and the 8255 is a parallel port.

questions.questionText: What do the AD0–AD7 lines of the 8085 carry during T2 and T3 of a memory write machine cycle?
options: The data byte being written, driven by the processor
The status bits S0 and S1
Nothing; they are always in high impedance
questions.explanation: In T1 AD0–AD7 carry A0–A7 (latched by ALE); from T2 onward they switch to data, driven out by the 8085 in a write and read in by it during a read.

questions.questionText: In the 8085, IO/M = 1 and RD = 0. The operation taking place is:
questions.explanation: IO/M = 1 selects an I/O port and an active-low RD means data is being read, so this is an I/O read cycle such as the third cycle of IN.

questions.questionText: During the opcode fetch machine cycle of the 8085, the status signals IO/M, S1 and S0 are:
questions.explanation: Opcode fetch is a memory access (IO/M = 0) with S1 = S0 = 1. 0 1 0 is a memory read, 0 0 1 a memory write and 1 1 1 an interrupt acknowledge.

questions.questionText: The last machine cycle of the 8085 instruction STA 2050H is a:
options: memory read with IO/M, S1, S0 = 0, 1, 0
I/O write with IO/M, S1, S0 = 1, 0, 1
memory write with IO/M, S1, S0 = 0, 0, 1
opcode fetch with IO/M, S1, S0 = 0, 1, 1
questions.explanation: STA = opcode fetch, two memory reads for the address bytes, then a memory write that stores A at 2050H. Memory write status is IO/M = 0, S1 = 0, S0 = 1.

questions.questionText: The correct sequence of machine cycles for the 8085 instruction MVI M, 25H is:
options: Opcode fetch, memory read, memory write
Opcode fetch, memory read, memory read
Opcode fetch, I/O read, memory write
questions.explanation: After the opcode fetch the data byte 25H is read from program memory (memory read), then written to the location addressed by HL (memory write): 4 + 3 + 3 = 10 T.

questions.questionText: Which of the following 8085 instructions has an opcode fetch cycle of 6 T-states instead of 4?
questions.explanation: Instructions that perform a 16-bit register operation during the fetch (INX, DCX, SPHL, PCHL) and those that must pre-decrement SP (PUSH, CALL, RST) use a 6-T opcode fetch. MOV A, B, MVI and LDA use the normal 4-T fetch.

questions.questionText: In which T-state of the 8085 opcode fetch cycle is the opcode decoded?
questions.explanation: T1 sends out the address with ALE, T2–T3 read the opcode into the instruction register with RD low, and T4 is used to decode it.

questions.questionText: What happens when a slow memory pulls the 8085 READY pin low?
options: The processor inserts wait states until READY returns high
The processor releases the buses for DMA
The processor raises a TRAP interrupt
questions.explanation: READY is sampled during T2; while it is low the 8085 adds wait states (each one T-state long), giving slow memory or I/O time to respond.

questions.questionText: The HOLD and HLDA pins of the 8085 are used for:
options: direct memory access (DMA) bus requests and grants
questions.explanation: A DMA controller raises HOLD to request the buses; the 8085 finishes its current machine cycle, floats its buses and replies with HLDA.

questions.questionText: Which 8085 pin is an output only?
questions.explanation: HLDA (hold acknowledge) is driven by the 8085. HOLD, READY and INTR are inputs driven by external devices.

questions.questionText: Which 8085 instruction reads the serial input bit on the SID pin?
questions.explanation: RIM loads bit 7 of the accumulator with the SID level (plus interrupt masks and pending bits). SIM sends A7 to the SOD pin; IN reads a whole byte from a port.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is NOT a flag of the 8085?
questions.explanation: The 8085 has only S, Z, AC, P and CY. An overflow flag (OF) appears in the 8086, not the 8085.

questions.questionText: What value does the program counter of the 8085 hold after RESET IN is activated?
questions.explanation: Reset clears the PC to 0000H, so a monitor or boot program must begin at that address. 0024H is the TRAP vector, not the reset address.

questions.questionText: Which statement about the 8085 stack is correct?
options: It is a set of eight on-chip registers that grows upwards
It lies in ROM and SP is loaded automatically at reset
It lies in read/write memory, grows towards lower addresses, and SP must be initialised by the program (e.g. LXI SP)
It grows towards higher addresses and each PUSH stores one byte
questions.explanation: The 8085 stack is simply part of external RAM. Each PUSH or CALL stores two bytes and moves SP down by 2; SP has no defined value after reset.

questions.questionText: Which pins of the 8085 carry only the higher-order address byte?
questions.explanation: A8–A15 are unidirectional address outputs; AD0–AD7 are shared between the low address byte and data.

subtopics.title: Intel 8086 Architecture
subtopics.subtitle: 16-bit pipelined CPU: BIU/EU, segment and general registers, 9 flags, modes, memory banks

concepts.text: Key Features of the 8086
The 8086 (1978, HMOS, about 29,000 transistors) is the first member of the x86 family:
items: 16-bit ALU, 16-bit registers and a 16-bit data bus; a 20-bit address bus gives 2^20 = 1 MB of memory (00000H–FFFFFH) plus a separate 64 KB I/O space.
40-pin DIP, +5 V supply, clock 5 MHz (8086), 8 MHz (8086-2) or 10 MHz (8086-1); the clock comes from the 8284 clock generator.
Address and data are multiplexed on AD0–AD15; A16/S3–A19/S6 carry the upper address bits and status. Every bus cycle takes 4 T-states (plus wait states).

Two internal units work in parallel and a 6-byte instruction queue lets the processor prefetch, which is why the 8086 is called pipelined. Supports the 8087 numeric coprocessor and multiprocessor operation in maximum mode.

concepts.text: Bus Interface Unit and Execution Unit

rows: Fetches instructions, reads and writes operands, forms 20-bit physical addresses
Decodes and executes instructions taken from the queue
CS, DS, SS, ES, IP, 6-byte prefetch queue, address adder
AX, BX, CX, DX, SP, BP, SI, DI, flag register, ALU, control circuitry
The only unit connected to the external bus
None; it asks the BIU for every memory or I/O access

concepts.text: While the EU executes one instruction, the BIU uses idle bus cycles to fetch the following bytes into the first-in first-out queue; a fetch happens whenever at least 2 bytes of the queue are empty. Fetch and execute therefore overlap, and the EU seldom waits for an opcode. On a jump, call or return the queue holds the wrong bytes, so it is flushed and refilled from the new address, which is the main penalty of branching.
Register Organisation

rows: Accumulator: implied operand of MUL, IMUL, DIV, IDIV, IN, OUT and string LODS/STOS
Base register: the only general register usable as a memory pointer, e.g. MOV AX, [BX]
Counter: LOOP, REP string prefixes; CL holds shift and rotate counts
Data: high word of 32-bit products and dividends (DX:AX); 16-bit port address in IN/OUT

concepts.text: Segment registers (16-bit, in the BIU) hold the upper 16 bits of the base address of a 64 KB segment:
items: CS (code segment): the segment of the program being executed; paired with IP.
DS (data segment): default segment for variables; paired with BX, SI, DI or a direct offset.
SS (stack segment): holds the stack; paired with SP (and BP).
ES (extra segment): a second data area, destination of string instructions; paired with DI.

concepts.text: Pointer and index registers (16-bit, offsets within a segment):
items: SP (stack pointer): offset of the top of stack in SS; PUSH subtracts 2, POP adds 2.
BP (base pointer): offset into the stack segment, used to reach parameters passed on the stack.
SI (source index) and DI (destination index): offsets for indexed addressing and for string operations (DS:SI → ES:DI).
IP (instruction pointer): offset of the next instruction in CS; the 8086 equivalent of the 8085 program counter.

concepts.text: Flag Register

rows: Carry out of, or borrow into, the most significant bit
The low byte of the result has even parity
Carry from bit 3 to bit 4 (BCD adjust)
The most significant bit of the result is 1
Signed result is out of range (carry into MSB ≠ carry out of MSB)

concepts.text: Three control flags are set by the program to change how the processor behaves rather than to report a result:
items: TF (Trap, bit 8): when 1 the processor single-steps, raising a type-1 interrupt after every instruction; used by debuggers.
IF (Interrupt enable, bit 9): 1 allows the INTR pin to be recognised (STI sets, CLI clears); NMI is unaffected.
DF (Direction, bit 10): 0 makes string instructions auto-increment SI/DI (CLD), 1 makes them auto-decrement (STD).
Total: 9 flags = 6 status (CF PF AF ZF SF OF) + 3 control (TF IF DF); bits 1, 3, 5 and 12–15 are unused.

concepts.text: Operating Modes, 8086 vs 8088, Memory Banks

Pin 33, MN/MX, selects the mode. In minimum mode (MN/MX = 1) the 8086 is the only processor and itself generates the control signals RD, WR, M/IO, DT/R, DEN, ALE, INTA and HOLD/HLDA; suited to small single-CPU systems. In maximum mode (MN/MX = 0) those pins become status lines S0–S2 and the 8288 bus controller decodes them into bus commands, while RQ/GT0–1 and LOCK support bus sharing with a coprocessor (8087) or other processors.
The 1 MB memory is split into two 512 KB banks so that a 16-bit word can be read in one bus cycle:
items: Even bank (A0 = 0) is connected to D0-D7 and holds even addresses; odd bank (BHE = 0) is connected to D8-D15 and holds odd addresses.
BHE = 0, A0 = 0: whole word from an even address using both banks in one bus cycle.
BHE = 1, A0 = 0: one byte from the even bank on D0-D7. BHE = 0, A0 = 1: one byte from the odd bank on D8-D15. BHE = 1, A0 = 1: no transfer.
Words are stored little-endian (low byte at the lower address). A word at an odd address spans both banks and needs two bus cycles; aligned words at even addresses need one.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Inside the 8086

The prefetch queue pays off because many instructions spend more clock cycles inside the EU than the bus needs to fetch the next bytes. The BIU uses those free bus cycles to keep the queue topped up, so the EU usually finds its next opcode already waiting. The gain disappears after every taken jump, call, return or interrupt, and also when an instruction needs many memory operands, because then the BIU is busy serving the EU instead of prefetching.

Time ->   | slot 1   | slot 2   | slot 3   | slot 4
BIU       | fetch I1 | fetch I2 | fetch I3 | fetch I4
EU        |  (wait)  | exec I1  | exec I2  | exec I3

JMP in I2 -> queue flushed, I3/I4 discarded
BIU       | fetch target T1 ... EU waits one slot again
Worked Example: Flags After an Addition

MOV AL, 7FH     ; AL = 0111 1111 (+127)
MOV BL, 01H     ; BL = 0000 0001 (+1)
ADD AL, BL      ; AL = 1000 0000 = 80H
; CF = 0  no carry out of bit 7
; OF = 1  +127 + 1 = +128 does not fit in 8-bit signed
; SF = 1  bit 7 of result is 1
; ZF = 0  result not zero
; AF = 1  F + 1 carries from bit 3 to bit 4
; PF = 0  80H has one 1-bit (odd parity)

CF and OF answer different questions. CF treats the operands as unsigned and reports a carry out of (or borrow into) the MSB; OF treats them as signed and is set when the carry into the MSB differs from the carry out of it. In the example above the unsigned sum 127 + 1 = 128 is fine (CF = 0) but the signed result overflows (OF = 1). PF looks only at the low byte of the result, even in 16-bit operations.

concepts.plainText: t_bus = (4 + Nw) / f_clk, where Nw is the number of wait states

concepts.text:
Word read from odd address 12345H, 5 MHz, no waits
Cycle 1: address 12345H, BHE = 0, A0 = 1
         byte 12345H (low byte) on D8-D15
Cycle 2: address 12346H, BHE = 1, A0 = 0
         byte 12346H (high byte) on D0-D7
Time = 2 x 4 x 200 ns = 1.6 us  (aligned word: 0.8 us)

Designing the memory follows directly from the two banks. Divide the required capacity by 2 to get the size of each bank, then divide by the chip capacity to get chips per bank. The chips' address inputs connect to A1 upwards, not A0, because A0 and BHE act as the bank selects. For example, 128 KB from 16K × 8 chips needs 4 chips per bank, 8 in total, with A1–A14 on the chip address pins.
Common mistakes with 8086 architecture questions:
items: Putting IP or the segment registers in the EU; they belong to the BIU with the queue.
Saying the queue refills when 1 byte is free (that is the 8088) instead of 2 bytes.
Using A0–A18 for bank addressing; each bank sees A1–A19.
Assuming INC and DEC change CF; they change all status flags except CF.
Forgetting that CMP and TEST change only the flags, never the destination operand.

concepts.text: For BHE/A0 questions, look at the last hex digit of the address: even means A0 = 0 and the even bank on D0–D7; odd means A0 = 1, BHE = 0 and the odd bank on D8–D15. A word at an even address uses BHE = 0 and A0 = 0 in one cycle.

formulas.plainText: One bus cycle = 4 T-states = 4 / f_clk (800 ns at 5 MHz)
9 flags = 6 status (CF PF AF ZF SF OF) + 3 control (TF IF DF)

notes.text: BIU fetches, EU executes; the overlap of the two is what 'pipelining in the 8086' means. Queue: 6 bytes on the 8086, 4 bytes on the 8088.

Do not swap the register roles: CX (not AX) counts loops and string repeats, DX (not BX) holds the high word of a 32-bit product and the port number for IN/OUT, and only BX among the general registers can hold a memory address.
At reset the 8086 sets CS = FFFFH and IP = 0000H, so the first instruction is fetched from physical address FFFF0H; DS, SS, ES and the flags are cleared and the queue is empty.

formulas.title: 8086 memory capacity
formulas.description: Twenty address lines A0–A19 give the 8086 a 1 MB physical address space from 00000H to FFFFFH.

formulas.title: Bus cycle time
formulas.description: Each 8086 bus cycle (T1–T4) takes four clock periods without wait states: 800 ns at 5 MHz.

formulas.title: Reset address
formulas.description: After reset CS = FFFFH and IP = 0000H, so execution starts 16 bytes below the top of the 1 MB map.

flashcards.front: Which registers belong to the BIU and which to the EU of the 8086?
flashcards.back: BIU: CS, DS, SS, ES, IP and the 6-byte queue. EU: AX, BX, CX, DX, SP, BP, SI, DI, the flags and the ALU.

flashcards.front: Name the six status flags and three control flags of the 8086.
flashcards.back: Status: CF, PF, AF, ZF, SF, OF. Control: TF (trap/single-step), IF (interrupt enable), DF (direction of string operations).

flashcards.front: What is the difference between minimum and maximum mode?
flashcards.back: Minimum mode (MN/MX = 1): single processor, the 8086 generates its own control signals. Maximum mode (MN/MX = 0): multiprocessor or coprocessor systems, the 8288 bus controller decodes status lines S0–S2 into bus commands.

flashcards.front: How does the 8086 access a 16-bit word stored at an odd address?
flashcards.back: It needs two bus cycles: one byte from the odd bank (BHE = 0, A0 = 1) and the other from the even bank at the next address. Words at even addresses are read in one cycle using both banks.

questions.questionText: Which functional unit of the 8086 forms the 20-bit physical address placed on the address bus?
questions.explanation: The BIU contains the segment registers, IP and the address adder that computes segment × 10H + offset; the EU only produces 16-bit offsets.

questions.questionText: Which of the following 8086 registers is located in the Bus Interface Unit?
questions.explanation: The BIU holds CS, DS, SS, ES, IP and the prefetch queue; SP, BP, SI and DI are pointer/index registers of the EU.

questions.questionText: How many flags are defined in the 8086 flag register?
questions.explanation: The 8086 has CF, PF, AF, ZF, SF, OF (status) and TF, IF, DF (control) = 9 flags; the other 7 bits are unused.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is a control flag of the 8086 rather than a status flag?
questions.explanation: DF (direction), IF (interrupt enable) and TF (trap) are set by the programmer to control operation; CF, AF and PF report results.

questions.questionText: What is the width of the external data bus of the 8086?
questions.explanation: The 8086 transfers data on AD0–AD15, a 16-bit bus; 20 bits is the width of its address bus, and 8 bits is the 8088's external data bus.

questions.questionText: The MN/MX pin of an 8086 is connected to +5 V. In which mode does the processor operate?
questions.explanation: MN/MX = 1 selects minimum mode, where the 8086 generates its own bus control signals for a single-processor system.

questions.questionText: Which support chip decodes the status lines S0–S2 into bus command signals when the 8086 runs in maximum mode?
questions.explanation: In maximum mode the 8288 bus controller converts S0–S2 into MRDC, MWTC, IORC, IOWC, INTA and ALE.

questions.questionText: Which 8086 flag, when set to 1, makes the processor execute one instruction and then generate a type-1 interrupt?
questions.explanation: TF enables single-step mode; after each instruction a type-1 interrupt occurs, which debuggers use to trace programs.

questions.questionText: The instruction pointer (IP) of the 8086 performs the same job as which 8085 register?
questions.explanation: IP holds the offset of the next instruction to be fetched from the code segment, just as the 8085 PC holds the address of the next instruction.

questions.questionText: In an 8086 system, the even memory bank is connected to which data lines?
questions.explanation: The even bank (selected by A0 = 0) holds even addresses and drives the lower data byte D0–D7; the odd bank drives D8–D15.

questions.questionText: How does the 8086 store a 16-bit word in memory?
options: Low byte at the lower address, high byte at the next higher address
High byte at the lower address, low byte at the next higher address
Both bytes at the same address in two separate banks
Low byte in the even bank and high byte in the odd bank, whatever the address
questions.explanation: The 8086 is little-endian: the least significant byte goes to the lower address. For odd addresses the low byte is in the odd bank, so the last option is wrong.

questions.questionText: Which 8086 instruction clears the direction flag so that string instructions auto-increment SI and DI?
questions.explanation: CLD makes DF = 0 (auto-increment); STD sets DF, CLI clears IF and CLC clears CF.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of the ALE signal of the 8086 in minimum mode?
options: To enable the data bus transceivers
To select between memory and I/O
To latch the address from the multiplexed AD0–AD15 lines during T1
questions.explanation: ALE pulses high in T1 so external latches (8282/74LS373) capture the address before the AD lines switch to data; DEN enables transceivers and M/IO selects memory or I/O.

questions.questionText: An 8086 register AX holds 3A7FH. What are the contents of AH and AL?
questions.explanation: AH is the high byte (bits 15–8) = 3AH and AL is the low byte (bits 7–0) = 7FH.

questions.questionText: When does the BIU of the 8086 fetch the next instruction bytes into its 6-byte queue?
options: Only when the queue is completely empty
When at least 2 bytes of the queue are empty
When at least 1 byte of the queue is empty
Only after the EU finishes the current instruction
questions.explanation: The 8086 fetches a 16-bit word at a time, so it refills the queue whenever 2 bytes are free; the 8088 (8-bit bus) refills when 1 byte is free.

questions.questionText: Which of the following 8086 instructions causes the instruction queue to be discarded and refilled?
questions.explanation: A jump changes IP, so the prefetched bytes belong to the wrong path; the queue is flushed and refilled from the new address. Sequential instructions keep the queue.

questions.questionText: Which statement correctly describes pipelining in the 8086?
options: The BIU fetches the next instructions while the EU executes the current one
The EU executes two instructions at the same time in separate ALUs
The BIU decodes instructions while the EU fetches operands
Each instruction is split into five stages that run in parallel
questions.explanation: Pipelining in the 8086 is the overlap of fetch (BIU, into the queue) and execute (EU); there is only one ALU and no multi-stage pipeline.

questions.questionText: Which flag occupies bit 11 of the 8086 flag register?
questions.explanation: Bit positions: CF 0, PF 2, AF 4, ZF 6, SF 7, TF 8, IF 9, DF 10, OF 11.

questions.questionText: An 8086 runs at 8 MHz with no wait states. How long does one bus cycle take?
questions.explanation: One bus cycle = 4 T-states = 4 / 8 MHz = 4 × 125 ns = 500 ns. 125 ns is a single T-state; 800 ns is the 5 MHz value.

questions.questionText: An 8086 runs at 10 MHz and the memory needs 2 wait states. How long does one memory read bus cycle take?
questions.explanation: t = (4 + 2) × 100 ns = 600 ns. 400 ns ignores the wait states and 200 ns counts only the wait states.

questions.questionText: The 8086 reads a single byte from physical address 20001H. What are the levels of BHE and A0 during this bus cycle?
questions.explanation: 20001H is odd, so A0 = 1 and the odd bank must be enabled with BHE = 0; the byte arrives on D8–D15.

questions.questionText: The 8086 reads a 16-bit word starting at physical address 30000H. Which statement is correct?
options: Two bus cycles, first with BHE = 0 and A0 = 1
One bus cycle with BHE = 1 and A0 = 0
One bus cycle with BHE = 0 and A0 = 0
Two bus cycles, first with BHE = 1 and A0 = 0
questions.explanation: 30000H is even (aligned), so both banks are enabled together (BHE = 0, A0 = 0) and the whole word moves in one bus cycle.

questions.questionText: In an 8086 system, in which memory bank is the byte at physical address 3A7F5H, and on which data lines is it transferred?
questions.explanation: The last hex digit 5 is odd, so A0 = 1: the byte is in the odd bank, enabled by BHE = 0, which is wired to D8–D15.

questions.questionText: The 8086 memory is divided into two banks. What is the size of each bank and which address lines select a location within a bank?
questions.explanation: 1 MB / 2 = 512 KB per bank = 2^19 locations, addressed by the 19 lines A1–A19; A0 and BHE choose the bank.

questions.questionText: Which of the following 8086 instructions is NOT valid?
questions.explanation: Only BX, BP, SI and DI can hold a memory offset in 8086 register-indirect addressing; CX cannot be used as a pointer.

questions.questionText: Which of the following signals is NOT produced directly by the 8086 when it operates in minimum mode?
questions.explanation: In minimum mode the 8086 itself drives ALE, DEN, DT/R, RD, WR, M/IO and INTA. MRDC (memory read command) is an output of the 8288 bus controller used in maximum mode.

questions.questionText: What are the RQ/GT0 and RQ/GT1 pins of the 8086 used for?
options: Bus request and grant between the 8086 and other bus masters in maximum mode
Requesting and granting interrupts in minimum mode
Selecting the upper and lower memory banks
Controlling the direction of the data transceivers
questions.explanation: In maximum mode RQ/GT lines replace HOLD/HLDA and let a coprocessor such as the 8087 request and be granted the local bus.

questions.questionText: What does the LOCK signal of the 8086 (active when an instruction has the LOCK prefix) do?
options: Disables all maskable and non-maskable interrupts
Prevents other bus masters from taking the bus until the locked instruction finishes
Freezes the instruction queue until the next jump
Locks the segment registers so they cannot be changed
questions.explanation: LOCK is used in maximum-mode multiprocessor systems to make read-modify-write sequences (e.g. XCHG on a semaphore) atomic; it does not affect interrupts.

questions.questionText: Which statement comparing the 8086 and the 8088 is NOT correct?
options: The 8088 has an 8-bit external data bus
The 8088 can address only 64 KB of memory
Both processors have the same registers and instruction set
questions.explanation: Both have 20 address lines and address 1 MB; the differences are the external data bus (16 vs 8 bits), the queue (6 vs 4 bytes) and a few pins such as BHE/SS0.

questions.questionText: After a reset, from which physical address does the 8086 fetch its first instruction?
questions.explanation: Reset loads CS = FFFFH and IP = 0000H, so PA = FFFF0H + 0000H = FFFF0H, 16 bytes below the top of memory.

questions.questionText: An 8086 program must read port 3F8H. Which instruction form must be used?
questions.explanation: Direct port addressing takes only an 8-bit port number (00H–FFH). Ports above FFH need the port address in DX, and the data register must be AL or AX.

questions.questionText: Which register holds the shift count when an 8086 instruction shifts AX by more than one position, as in SHL AX, CL?
questions.explanation: For multi-bit shifts and rotates the 8086 takes the count from CL; a count of 1 can be coded as an immediate.

questions.questionText: An 8086 program executes CLI. Which interrupt requests can still be recognised?
options: INTR and NMI but not INT n
questions.explanation: CLI clears IF, which masks only the INTR pin; NMI is non-maskable and INT n instructions are executed regardless of IF.

questions.questionText: On the 8086, DF = 1 when MOVSB is executed. What happens to SI and DI after the byte is moved?
options: SI is incremented and DI is decremented
questions.explanation: DF = 1 selects auto-decrement; a byte string instruction changes SI and DI by 1 (by 2 for word instructions such as MOVSW).

questions.questionText: On the 8086, SP = 2000H. The instructions PUSH AX, PUSH BX and POP CX are executed in that order. What is SP afterwards?
questions.explanation: Each PUSH subtracts 2 and each POP adds 2: 2000H − 2 − 2 + 2 = 1FFEH.

questions.questionText: Which kind of address does the Execution Unit of the 8086 compute and pass to the BIU for a memory operand?
questions.explanation: The EU calculates only the offset (effective address) from the addressing mode; the BIU adds segment × 10H to form the 20-bit physical address.

questions.questionText: On the 8086, AL = 7FH and BL = 01H. After ADD AL, BL, which set of results is correct?
questions.explanation: 7FH + 01H = 80H with no carry out (CF = 0). Two positive numbers gave a negative result, so OF = 1; bit 7 is 1 so SF = 1; 80H has one 1-bit (odd) so PF = 0.

questions.questionText: The 8086 flag register contains 0A85H. Which flags are set?
questions.explanation: 0A85H = 0000 1010 1000 0101: bits 0, 2, 7, 9 and 11 are 1, which are CF, PF, SF, IF and OF.

questions.questionText: The 8086 reads a 16-bit word from odd physical address 12345H. How is the access carried out?
options: One bus cycle with BHE = 0 and A0 = 1, both bytes on D0–D15
Two bus cycles: byte at 12345H from the odd bank on D8–D15 (BHE = 0, A0 = 1), then byte at 12346H from the even bank on D0–D7 (BHE = 1, A0 = 0)
Two bus cycles: byte at 12344H from the even bank, then byte at 12345H from the odd bank
Two bus cycles: byte at 12345H from the even bank on D0–D7, then byte at 12346H from the odd bank on D8–D15
questions.explanation: A misaligned word spans both banks at different A1–A19 values, so it needs two cycles: the low byte (12345H, odd) via D8–D15, then the high byte (12346H, even) via D0–D7.

questions.questionText: An 8086 system needs 128 KB of RAM built from 16K × 8 chips. How many chips go in each bank, and which processor address lines drive the chips' address inputs?
questions.explanation: Each bank holds 128 KB / 2 = 64 KB = 4 chips of 16 KB. A 16K chip needs 14 address lines; since A0 selects the bank, they are A1–A14.

questions.questionText: On the 8086, AX = 0100H and BX = 0200H. After MUL BX, what do DX and AX contain?
questions.explanation: 0100H × 0200H = 256 × 512 = 131072 = 00020000H; the high word 0002H goes to DX and the low word 0000H to AX (CF = OF = 1 because DX ≠ 0).

questions.questionText: On the 8086, AL = 05H and BL = 07H. After CMP AL, BL, which statement is correct?
questions.explanation: CMP computes 05H − 07H = FEH without storing it, so AL stays 05H. A borrow occurs (CF = 1), the result is non-zero (ZF = 0) and bit 7 of FEH is 1 (SF = 1).

questions.questionText: On the 8086, AX = 1234H is stored as a word at physical address 20000H. Where is the byte 12H held, and on which data lines is it transferred?
options: At 20001H in the odd bank, on D8–D15
At 20000H in the even bank, on D0–D7
At 20001H in the even bank, on D0–D7
At 20000H in the odd bank, on D8–D15
questions.explanation: Little-endian storage puts the low byte 34H at 20000H (even bank, D0–D7) and the high byte 12H at 20001H (odd bank, D8–D15); both move in one bus cycle.

questions.questionText: On the 8086, AL = 38H and BL = 29H. After ADD AL, BL, what are AL, AF and PF?
questions.explanation: 38H + 29H = 61H. The low nibbles 8 + 9 = 17 exceed 15, so a carry passes from bit 3 to bit 4 (AF = 1). 61H = 0110 0001 has three 1-bits (odd), so PF = 0. 67H is the decimal sum 38 + 29.

questions.questionText: An 8086 at 8 MHz (no wait states) reads an array of 50 words. How much time is saved if the array starts at an even address instead of an odd address?
questions.explanation: Odd-aligned: 50 × 2 cycles × 500 ns = 50 µs. Even-aligned: 50 × 1 × 500 ns = 25 µs. Saving = 25 µs. 50 µs is the total misaligned time, not the saving.

subtopics.title: Segment:Offset & Physical Address Calculation
subtopics.subtitle: How the 8086 turns two 16-bit values into a 20-bit address, with worked examples

concepts.text: Why the 8086 Uses Segmentation

Every 8086 register is 16 bits wide, yet the address bus has 20 bits. The processor bridges the gap by dividing the 1 MB memory into segments of at most 64 KB. A segment must begin at an address divisible by 16 (a paragraph boundary), so its 20-bit base always ends in a hex 0 and the upper 16 bits alone identify it; that value is what a segment register holds. Any byte inside the segment is then located by a 16-bit offset (also called the effective address) from the segment base.

concepts.plainText: Physical address = Segment × 10H + Offset (shift segment left 4 bits, then add)

concepts.text: Logical vs Physical Address

A logical address is the pair the program works with, written segment:offset, e.g. 1234H:0022H. The physical address is the single 20-bit number the BIU places on the address bus: 12340H + 0022H = 12362H. The programmer and the assembler deal only in logical addresses, which is what allows a program to be loaded anywhere in memory simply by changing the segment register values. Because the segment can be chosen in many ways, one physical address corresponds to many different logical addresses.

rows: PUSH, POP, CALL, RET, interrupt stack frames
Destination of string instructions (MOVS, STOS, SCAS)

concepts.text: Worked Examples

; 1. Instruction fetch
;    CS = 3400H, IP = 0120H
;    PA = 34000H + 0120H = 34120H

; 2. Data byte via BX
;    DS = 1234H, BX = 0022H
;    PA = 12340H + 0022H = 12362H

; 3. Top of stack
;    SS = 5000H, SP = FFFEH
;    PA = 50000H + FFFEH = 5FFFEH

; 4. String destination
;    ES = B800H, DI = 0A00H
;    PA = B8000H + 0A00H = B8A00H

; 5. Wrap-around at the top of memory
;    CS = FFFFH, IP = 0010H
;    FFFF0H + 0010H = 100000H -> A20 dropped -> 00000H

Limits of a segment: the lowest address is Segment × 10H (offset 0000H) and the highest is Segment × 10H + FFFFH (offset FFFFH). For DS = 2A00H the data segment runs from 2A000H to 39FFFH. Because the base is a multiple of 16 and the size is 64 KB, a segment is fully described by its 16-bit register value alone.

concepts.plainText: Segment end = Segment × 10H + FFFFH (64 KB above the base)

concepts.text: Reverse problems ask for a logical address of a given physical address. Physical 12345H can be written 1234H:0005H, 1000H:2345H, 1230H:0045H or 0234H:F005H, all valid because each segment value is a multiple-of-16 base at or below 12345H and within 64 KB of it. To get the offset for a chosen segment, compute Offset = PA − Segment × 10H; it must fall between 0000H and FFFFH.
Overlapping Segments

Only the starting address of a segment is restricted, so the four active segments can be placed anywhere: disjoint, adjacent, partly overlapping or exactly on top of each other. The minimum distance between two different segment bases is 16 bytes, and 2^16 = 65536 distinct bases are possible. Small programs (COM files) put CS, DS, SS and ES all equal so that code, data and stack share one 64 KB segment; large programs give each its own area.
Advantages of Segmentation
Why the 8086 designers chose segmentation:
items: Lets 16-bit registers and 16-bit arithmetic address the full 1 MB memory.
Programs are relocatable: to move a program, only the segment register values change; every offset inside stays the same.
Code, data and stack are logically separated, which supports modular programming and simple protection against one area corrupting another.
Each 64 KB segment is compact enough for 16-bit offsets, so instructions stay short.
