At reset CS:IP = FFFFH:0000H = FFFF0H, so the system ROM is placed at the top of memory and the interrupt vector table at the bottom (00000H–003FFH).

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Address Arithmetic

Inside the BIU a dedicated 20-bit adder forms every physical address. The 16-bit segment value enters shifted four places left, so its bits land on positions 4–19 and the low four bits are zero; the 16-bit offset enters unshifted on positions 0–15. Only the middle twelve bits overlap, so a carry can ripple into the top hex digit but never beyond bit 19, because there is no bit 20 on the 8086.

Example 1: DS = 1A2BH, BX = 3C4DH
  1A2B0   (segment, shifted)
+ 03C4D   (offset, right-aligned)
-------
  1DEFD   -> PA = 1DEFDH

Example 2: CS = 2F00H, IP = FFF0H
  2F000 + 0FFF0 = 3EFF0H  (carry into 5th digit)

concepts.plainText: ceil((PA − FFFFH) / 10H) ≤ Seg ≤ floor(PA / 10H): all segment values that can reach PA

concepts.text:
Reverse problem: logical addresses for PA = 4F2A6H
Largest Seg  = floor(4F2A6H / 10H)          = 4F2AH -> offset 0006H
Smallest Seg = ceil((4F2A6H - FFFFH) / 10H)
             = ceil(3F2A7H / 10H)          = 3F2BH -> offset FFF6H
Check: 3F2B0H + FFF6H = 4F2A6H
Count = 4F2AH - 3F2BH + 1 = 1000H = 4096 pairs

Ignoring wrap-around, every physical address from 0FFF0H to FFFFFH has exactly 4096 logical addresses, because a 64 KB offset range spans 4096 paragraph boundaries. Addresses near the bottom of memory have fewer, since the segment cannot go below 0000H; for example PA 00020H is reached without wrap-around only through segments 0000H, 0001H and 0002H.

rows: Operand via BX, SI, DI or direct address

concepts.plainText: Overlap = 10000H − (Seg2 − Seg1) × 10H bytes, valid when Seg2 − Seg1 < 1000H (both 64 KB long)

concepts.text:
; SS = 5000H, SP = 2000H, AX = ABCDH
PUSH AX    ; SP = 1FFEH, CDH -> 51FFEH, ABH -> 51FFFH
PUSH BX    ; SP = 1FFCH, top of stack at 51FFCH
POP  CX    ; CX = old BX, SP = 1FFEH
POP  DX    ; DX = ABCDH, SP = 2000H
; SP wraps inside the segment: SP = 0000H, PUSH -> SP = FFFEH
; the word goes to SS:FFFEH, never into the segment below

Wrap-around happens at two levels. An offset that passes FFFFH wraps back to 0000H inside the same segment, which is why a PUSH with SP = 0000H writes at SS:FFFEH. A physical address that passes FFFFFH loses its carry and wraps to the bottom of memory, so FFFFH:0010H is 00000H and FFFFH:0020H is 00010H. Later processors (80286 onwards) have an A20 line and can reach 100000H–10FFEFH in real mode when A20 is enabled; the 8086 cannot.
Common mistakes in address calculation:
items: Adding segment and offset without the shift (1A2BH + 3C4DH = 5678H).
Shifting the offset instead of the segment.
Using DS for [BP]-based operands; BP defaults to SS.
Using DS for the destination of a string instruction; it is always ES:DI.
Answering 17000H for the last byte of a 3000H-byte block at 14000H; the last offset is size − 1.

concepts.text: In reverse questions, check each option by recomputing Seg × 10H + Offset rather than trying to solve backwards; it takes seconds and catches options with a wrong shift or an offset larger than FFFFH.

formulas.plainText: Segment range = Seg × 10H to Seg × 10H + FFFFH

notes.text: Append one hex 0 to the segment, then add the offset: 2A00H:0100H → 2A000H + 0100H = 2A100H. Line the numbers up on the right before adding; carries into the fifth digit are normal.
Adding without shifting (2A00H + 0100H = 2B00H) and shifting the offset instead of the segment are the two classic wrong options; both will always appear among the choices.
There is no address 100000H: any physical address above FFFFFH wraps around to the bottom of memory because the 8086 has only 20 address lines.

formulas.title: 8086 physical address
formulas.description: The 20-bit physical address from a 16-bit segment register and a 16-bit offset; e.g. 1234H:0022H → 12362H.

formulas.title: Segment size
formulas.description: The largest range a 16-bit offset can cover; a segment may be smaller but never larger.

formulas.title: Offset from physical address
formulas.description: Reverse calculation for a chosen segment value; the result must lie between 0000H and FFFFH.

formulas.title: Number of possible segment bases
formulas.description: Segments start on 16-byte paragraph boundaries, so there are 65536 possible segment starting addresses in 1 MB.

flashcards.front: Compute the physical address for SS = 5000H, SP = FFFEH.
flashcards.back: PA = 5000H × 10H + FFFEH = 50000H + FFFEH = 5FFFEH.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a logical and a physical address in the 8086?
flashcards.back: A logical address is the segment:offset pair the program uses (two 16-bit values); the physical address is the single 20-bit value put on the address bus, equal to segment × 10H + offset.

flashcards.front: Why must an 8086 segment start at an address divisible by 16?
flashcards.back: Because the 20-bit base is formed by shifting the 16-bit segment register left by 4 bits, its low hex digit is always 0; only multiples of 16 (paragraph boundaries) can be represented.

flashcards.front: Give two advantages of segmented memory in the 8086.
flashcards.back: 16-bit registers can reach 1 MB of memory, and programs are relocatable by changing only the segment registers; it also separates code, data and stack.

questions.questionText: An 8086 has CS = 4A00H and IP = 0123H. From which physical address is the next instruction fetched?
questions.explanation: PA = 4A00H × 10H + 0123H = 4A000H + 0123H = 4A123H. 4B23H comes from adding without shifting the segment.

questions.questionText: Which segment register is always used with IP to fetch 8086 instructions?
questions.explanation: The instruction fetch address is always CS:IP; this pairing cannot be changed by a segment override prefix.

questions.questionText: Which segment register does the 8086 use by default with SP for PUSH and POP?
questions.explanation: Stack operations always address SS:SP.

questions.questionText: In 8086 string instructions such as MOVSB or STOSB, the destination operand is addressed by which pair?
questions.explanation: String sources default to DS:SI and destinations always use ES:DI.

questions.questionText: An 8086 segment must begin at a physical address that is:
questions.explanation: The base is the 16-bit segment value shifted left 4 bits, so its lowest hex digit is always 0, i.e. a multiple of 16.

questions.questionText: In the 8086, what is a logical address?
options: The 20-bit value placed on the address bus
The offset alone, without a segment
A segment:offset pair of two 16-bit values used by the program
The address after the A20 line is dropped
questions.explanation: A logical address is written segment:offset (for example 2000H:0150H); the BIU converts it into the 20-bit physical address.

questions.questionText: On the 8086, DS = 2500H. What is the starting physical address of the data segment?
On the 8086, SS = 7000H. What is the highest physical address that belongs to this stack segment?
questions.explanation: End = SS × 10H + FFFFH = 70000H + FFFFH = 7FFFFH.

questions.questionText: Appending one hexadecimal 0 to an 8086 segment value before adding the offset is the same as:
questions.explanation: One hex digit is 4 bits, and shifting left by 4 bits multiplies by 2^4 = 16 (10H).

questions.questionText: An 8086 program is moved to a different area of memory. What has to change so that it still runs correctly?
options: Both the segment values and all offsets
The physical addresses coded into every instruction
questions.explanation: Offsets are relative to the segment base, so a relocated program keeps its offsets; loading new segment values is enough.

questions.questionText: Which value must be loaded into DS so that the 8086 data segment starts at physical address 8A000H?
questions.explanation: Segment = starting address ÷ 10H = 8A000H ÷ 10H = 8A00H. 8A000H is 20 bits and cannot fit a segment register.

questions.questionText: On the 8086, DS = 0000H. What is the highest physical address a data access through DS can reach?
questions.explanation: Highest = 0000H × 10H + FFFFH = 0FFFFH, the top of the first 64 KB.

questions.questionText: In 8086 terminology, the 'effective address' of a memory operand is:
options: the address of the instruction that uses it
questions.explanation: The EU computes the effective address (offset) from the addressing mode; adding the segment base gives the physical address.

questions.questionText: Which segment:offset pair does the 8086 use by default for the operand of MOV AL, [SI]?
questions.explanation: Register-indirect operands through SI (and BX, DI or a direct address) default to the data segment DS; only BP-based operands default to SS.

questions.questionText: On the 8086, DS = 1A2BH and BX = 3C4DH. What is the physical address of the operand in MOV AL, [BX]?
questions.explanation: PA = 1A2B0H + 3C4DH = 1DEFDH. 5678H is DS + BX without the shift; 3DEFBH (3C4D0H + 1A2BH) shifts BX instead of DS.

questions.questionText: On the 8086, SS = 6A00H and SP = 1F40H. What is the physical address of the top of the stack?
questions.explanation: PA = 6A000H + 1F40H = 6BF40H. 8940H ignores the shift; 7BF40H results from a wrong carry into the fifth digit.

questions.questionText: On the 8086, CS = 2F00H and IP = FFF0H. From which physical address is the next instruction fetched?
questions.explanation: PA = 2F000H + FFF0H = 3EFF0H; the carry from the fourth hex digit moves into the fifth digit (2 + 1 = 3).

questions.questionText: On the 8086, DS = 3000H, SS = 2000H and BP = 0100H. Which physical address does MOV AL, [BP+05H] read?
questions.explanation: Addressing through BP uses SS by default: PA = 20000H + 0100H + 05H = 20105H. 30105H wrongly uses DS.

questions.questionText: On the 8086, DS = 1000H, ES = 2000H and BX = 0050H. Which physical address does MOV AX, ES:[BX] read?
questions.explanation: The ES: override replaces the default DS: PA = 20000H + 0050H = 20050H. 10050H would be the address without the override.

questions.questionText: On the 8086, DS = 3A00H. What offset must be used to reach the byte at physical address 3B7A2H?
questions.explanation: Offset = PA − DS × 10H = 3B7A2H − 3A000H = 17A2H. Subtracting 3A00H without the shift gives 37DA2H, which is not even a 16-bit offset.

questions.questionText: An 8086 byte is at physical address 5A3F0H and its offset is 03F0H. What is the segment value?
questions.explanation: Segment = (PA − offset) ÷ 10H = (5A3F0H − 03F0H) ÷ 10H = 5A000H ÷ 10H = 5A00H. 5A3FH would need offset 0000H.

questions.questionText: Which 8086 logical address refers to physical address 4F2A6H?
questions.explanation: 4E00H:12A6H → 4E000H + 12A6H = 4F2A6H. The others give 4F300H, 51A60H and 402A6H.

questions.questionText: On the 8086 (20 address lines), DS = FFFFH and the offset is 0020H. Which physical address is actually accessed?
questions.explanation: FFFF0H + 0020H = 100010H, a 21-bit result. The 8086 has no A20 line, so the carry is lost and the access wraps to 00010H.

questions.questionText: On the 8086, SS = 1200H and SP = 0FFEH. After one POP BX, what is SP and what is the physical address of the new top of stack?
questions.explanation: POP adds 2: SP = 0FFEH + 2 = 1000H. Top of stack = 12000H + 1000H = 13000H. 0FFCH would be the result of a PUSH.

questions.questionText: On the 8086, DS = 1000H, SI = 0020H, ES = 2000H and DI = 0030H. MOVSB is executed. Which physical addresses are the source and destination bytes?
questions.explanation: Source = DS:SI = 10000H + 0020H = 10020H; destination = ES:DI = 20000H + 0030H = 20030H. Using DS for the destination is the common error.

questions.questionText: Which 8086 logical address refers to the same physical location as 0100H:0000H?
An 8086 program 12 KB long is loaded from offset 0000H in a code segment with CS = 1400H. What is the physical address of its last byte?
questions.explanation: 12 KB = 3000H bytes, so the last offset is 2FFFH. PA = 14000H + 2FFFH = 16FFFH. 17000H is one past the end.

questions.questionText: What is the maximum amount of memory an 8086 program can address at one moment without reloading any segment register, if its four segments do not overlap?
questions.explanation: Four segment registers × 64 KB each = 256 KB can be addressed without changing a segment register.

questions.questionText: On the 8086, CS = 1000H and DS = 2000H. How are the code and data segments placed relative to each other?
options: Adjacent: the code segment ends at 1FFFFH and the data segment begins at 20000H
questions.explanation: CS covers 10000H–1FFFFH and DS covers 20000H–2FFFFH, so they touch but do not overlap.

questions.questionText: What is the smallest possible distance between the starting addresses of two different 8086 segments?
questions.explanation: Consecutive segment values (e.g. 1000H and 1001H) give bases 10000H and 10010H, which are 10H = 16 bytes apart.

questions.questionText: How many different starting addresses can an 8086 segment have within the 1 MB memory?
questions.explanation: There are 2^20 / 2^4 = 2^16 = 65,536 paragraph boundaries, one for each 16-bit segment value.

questions.questionText: Why can an 8086 segment NOT start at physical address 12345H?
options: The address is not a multiple of 16, so no 16-bit segment value produces it
The address lies above the first 64 KB
Segments may only start at multiples of 64 KB
Odd addresses cannot be accessed by the 8086
questions.explanation: Base = segment × 10H always ends in hex 0; 12345H ends in 5. The data at 12345H can still be reached, for example as 1234H:0005H.

questions.questionText: Which default segment assignment of the 8086 can NOT be changed with a segment override prefix?
options: ES for the destination of STOSB
questions.explanation: String destinations always use ES:DI (and fetches always use CS:IP). Data references through BX, SI or BP can be overridden, e.g. ES:[BX].

questions.questionText: Which statement about 8086 segmentation is NOT correct?
options: A segment can be at most 64 KB long
Segments must not overlap each other
One physical address can be reached through many logical addresses
The four segment registers may all hold the same value
questions.explanation: Segments may be disjoint, adjacent, partly overlapping or identical; only their starting address (a multiple of 16) is restricted.

questions.questionText: An 8086 program must access the last byte of memory, FFFFFH, using offset FFFFH. Which segment value is required?
questions.explanation: Segment = (FFFFFH − FFFFH) ÷ 10H = F0000H ÷ 10H = F000H. With FFFFH the address would be FFFF0H + FFFFH, which wraps to 0FFEFH.

questions.questionText: On the 8086, CS = 3C00H. Which of the following physical addresses lies inside the current code segment?
questions.explanation: The code segment spans 3C000H to 3C000H + FFFFH = 4BFFFH. 3BFFFH is just below it, 4C000H just above it, and 03C00H is the segment value mistaken for an address.

questions.questionText: Which of the following 8086 logical addresses does NOT refer to physical address 2C3D8H?
questions.explanation: 1C00H:C3D8H → 1C000H + C3D8H = 283D8H. The others give 2C3D0H + 8, 20000H + C3D8H and 1C3E0H + FFF8H, all equal to 2C3D8H.

questions.questionText: How many different segment:offset pairs refer to the physical address 50000H on the 8086?
questions.explanation: Valid segments satisfy 0 ≤ 50000H − 16·Seg ≤ FFFFH, i.e. 4001H ≤ Seg ≤ 5000H: 5000H − 4001H + 1 = 1000H = 4,096 pairs.

questions.questionText: What is the full range of segment values that can be used to reach physical address 4F2A6H on the 8086?
questions.explanation: Largest: 4F2A6H ÷ 10H rounded down = 4F2AH (offset 0006H). Smallest: (4F2A6H − FFFFH) = 3F2A7H, ÷ 10H rounded up = 3F2BH (offset FFF6H). 3F2AH would need offset 10006H.

questions.questionText: On the 8086, DS = 2000H and ES = 2800H. How large is the region shared by the two segments, and where is it?
options: No overlap; the segments are adjacent
questions.explanation: DS spans 20000H–2FFFFH and ES spans 28000H–37FFFH. The common part is 28000H–2FFFFH = 8000H bytes = 32 KB.

questions.questionText: On an 8086, CS = F800H and IP = 9000H. From which physical address is the instruction actually fetched?
questions.explanation: F8000H + 9000H = 101000H, which needs 21 bits; the carry out of A19 is lost, so the fetch wraps around to 01000H.

questions.questionText: On the 8086, SS = 4000H and SP = 0000H. After PUSH AX, what is SP and where is the word stored?
questions.explanation: SP = 0000H − 2 wraps within 16 bits to FFFEH; the stack stays in its own segment, so PA = 40000H + FFFEH = 4FFFEH, not 3FFFEH.

questions.questionText: On the 8086, SS = 5000H and SP = 2000H. The instructions PUSH AX, PUSH BX, PUSH CX and POP DX are executed. What is SP and the physical address of the top of stack afterwards?
questions.explanation: Three pushes and one pop change SP by −6 + 2 = −4: SP = 1FFCH. PA = 50000H + 1FFCH = 51FFCH. 1FFAH forgets the POP.

questions.questionText: The top of an 8086 stack is at physical address 3A7FEH and SP = 7FEEH. What is the value of SS?
questions.explanation: SS × 10H = 3A7FEH − 7FEEH = 32810H, so SS = 3281H. 3A7FH would only be correct if SP were 000EH.

questions.questionText: On the 8086, DS = 0A00H. A program needs the byte at 0B234H and later the byte at 1B234H. Which statement is correct?
options: The first uses offset 1234H; the second cannot be reached without changing DS
questions.explanation: 0B234H − 0A000H = 1234H. 1B234H − 0A000H = 11234H, which exceeds FFFFH, so it lies outside this 64 KB segment; DS must be reloaded.

questions.questionText: On the 8086, SS = 3000H, SP = 0200H and AX = ABCDH. After PUSH AX, where are the two bytes of AX stored?
questions.explanation: SP becomes 01FEH. The word goes to 30000H + 01FEH = 301FEH in little-endian order: low byte CDH at 301FEH, high byte ABH at 301FFH.

subtopics.title: Addressing Modes (8085 & 8086)
subtopics.subtitle: How an instruction locates its operand: 8085 and 8086 modes, effective-address arithmetic

concepts.text: What an Addressing Mode Is

An addressing mode is the way an instruction specifies where its operand is: inside the instruction itself, in a register, at a fixed memory address, or at an address computed from registers and a displacement. The mode decides the instruction length, the number of machine cycles and, in the 8086, which segment register is used. Recognising the mode from the operand syntax is the whole skill: a number with no brackets is immediate, a register name is register, brackets mean memory.
8085 Addressing Modes

rows: In the instruction, right after the opcode
In a CPU register named by the opcode
At the memory address or port given in the instruction
MOV A, M / LDAX B / STAX D
At the memory address held in HL (M), BC or DE
Fixed by the opcode itself, usually the accumulator or carry flag

concepts.text: The length follows from the mode. Register and register-indirect instructions carry no operand bytes, so they are 1 byte. Immediate 8-bit data or an 8-bit port number adds one byte (2-byte instructions). A 16-bit address or 16-bit immediate data adds two bytes stored low byte first, giving 3-byte instructions such as LDA 2050H (3A 50 20) and LXI H, 2050H (21 50 20).
8086 Addressing Modes

rows: None; data is in the instruction
MOV AX, [2050H] or MOV AX, COUNT
EA = contents of BX, SI, DI or BP
EA = base + index + displacement; useful for 2-D arrays
Source DS:SI, destination ES:DI, auto-incremented or decremented by DF
8-bit port in the instruction (0–255) or 16-bit port in DX (0–65535)
JNZ AGAIN, JMP SHORT L1, LOOP TOP
No operand; the opcode names what is affected

concepts.plainText: EA = Base (BX or BP) + Index (SI or DI) + Displacement; each term optional

concepts.text: The BIU adds the effective address to a segment base. BX, SI, DI and direct addresses use DS by default; anything involving BP uses SS, because BP is meant to reach parameters on the stack; string destinations use ES:DI and IP always uses CS. A segment override prefix (ES:, CS:, SS:, DS:) such as MOV AX, ES:[BX] changes the default for one instruction, except that the string destination and the stack for PUSH/POP cannot be overridden.
Worked Effective-Address Calculations

; Given: DS = 2000H, SS = 3000H, BX = 1000H, SI = 0200H, BP = 0100H, DI = 0050H

MOV AX, [BX+SI+10H]   ; based-indexed with displacement
; EA = 1000H + 0200H + 0010H = 1210H
; PA = DS x 10H + EA = 20000H + 1210H = 21210H

MOV AX, [BP+4]        ; based, BP -> stack segment
; EA = 0100H + 0004H = 0104H
; PA = SS x 10H + EA = 30000H + 0104H = 30104H

MOV AL, [DI+2]        ; indexed
; EA = 0050H + 0002H = 0052H
; PA = 20000H + 0052H = 20052H

MOV CX, [1234H]       ; direct
; EA = 1234H, PA = 20000H + 1234H = 21234H

rows: About 11 including based, indexed, string, I/O and relative
HL (as M), BC and DE (LDAX/STAX only)
BX, BP, SI, DI in any combination of base + index
None; 16-bit address is the physical address
Default DS, SS for BP, ES for string destination, override prefixes allowed
MOV AL, 25H (2 bytes); MOV AX, 1234H (3 bytes)

concepts.text: Quick identification rules for MCQs:
items: No brackets and a constant → immediate; no brackets and a register → register.
Brackets with only a number or a variable name → direct.
Brackets with a single register and nothing else → register indirect.
Brackets with BX or BP plus a number → based; SI or DI plus a number → indexed; a base and an index together → based-indexed (with displacement if a number is added).

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Addressing Modes

In the 8086 the execution unit forms the effective address (EA) with a 16-bit adder: it adds whichever of base, index and displacement the instruction names, and an 8-bit displacement is first sign-extended, so [BX-2] is encoded as BX + FEH treated as −2. Any carry out of bit 15 is discarded, so the EA wraps around inside the 64 KB segment rather than spilling into the next one. The bus interface unit then adds the segment base (segment × 10H); on the 8086 a sum above FFFFFH wraps to the bottom of memory because only 20 address lines exist.

concepts.latex: EA = (B + I + d) \bmod 2^{16},\quad PA = (16 \cdot Seg + EA) \bmod 2^{20}
concepts.plainText: EA = (Base + Index + displacement) mod 65536; PA = (Segment × 16 + EA) mod 2^20

concepts.text: Relative addressing, used by JMP SHORT, the conditional jumps and LOOP, stores only a signed distance. By the time the jump executes, IP already points to the byte after the jump instruction, so the displacement is measured from there, not from the jump opcode. An 8-bit displacement therefore reaches from 128 bytes backward to 127 bytes forward of the next instruction, and because the code does not contain an absolute address it still works if the program is loaded elsewhere.

concepts.plainText: Target = IP of next instruction + sign-extended displacement; d = Target − (jump address + jump length)

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: word array MAT at offset 0600H, 8 words per row, DS = 1500H
Read MAT[3][5] (zero-based, row-major) with MOV AX, [BX+SI+0600H]
  bytes per row  = 8 words x 2         = 16 = 0010H
  BX (row part)  = 3 x 0010H           = 0030H
  SI (col part)  = 5 x 2               = 000AH
  EA             = 0030H + 000AH + 0600H = 063AH
  PA             = 1500H x 10H + 063AH   = 1563AH
Wraparound: BX = FFF8H, disp = 0010H -> EA = 10008H mod 10000H = 0008H
  with DS = 3000H the byte read is at 30008H, not 40008H

Worked example 2: backward JNZ (2-byte instruction, 8086)
  loop start AGAIN at CS:0300H, JNZ AGAIN placed at CS:0310H
  IP after fetching JNZ = 0310H + 2 = 0312H
  d = 0300H - 0312H = -12H
  -12H as an 8-bit two's complement = EEH
  encoded: 75 EE   (75H = JNZ opcode)
Check: 0312H + FFEEH (EEH sign-extended) = 0300H (carry out discarded)

; 8085 program at 2000H: mode, size, address of each instruction
        LXI H, 2050H   ; immediate (16-bit)  3 bytes  2000H
        MOV A, M       ; register indirect   1 byte   2003H
        INX H          ; register            1 byte   2004H
        ADD M          ; register indirect   1 byte   2005H
        CMA            ; implied             1 byte   2006H
        STA 2060H      ; direct              3 bytes  2007H
        HLT            ; implied             1 byte   200AH
; total = 11 bytes, occupying 2000H-200AH

rows: Memory, no displacement (r/m = 110 means direct address)

concepts.text: Common mistakes in address calculations:
items: Adding the segment value without multiplying it by 16 (shifting one hex digit left).
Using DS for an operand that contains BP; any BP form defaults to SS.
Forgetting to scale an array index by the element size (2 for words) before adding it.
Letting the effective address carry into the segment instead of wrapping it modulo 10000H.
Measuring a jump displacement from the jump opcode instead of from the next instruction.
Reading a word as high byte first; the byte at the lower address is always the low byte.

concepts.text: For any 8086 address question, write three lines: which registers form the EA, which segment is used (DS, or SS if BP appears, or the override), and PA = segment × 10H + EA. Most wrong options are the result of skipping one of these lines.

formulas.plainText: Relative jump target = address of next instruction + signed displacement

notes.text: MOV AX, 5 is immediate; MOV AX, [5] is direct memory. The brackets are the whole question. In the 8085, MVI is immediate and MOV is register; LDA is direct and MOV A, M is register indirect.
Any 8086 operand that contains BP is taken from the stack segment (SS), not DS. Also, BX+BP and SI+DI are illegal combinations: an address may contain at most one base and one index register.
Direct and immediate 8085 instructions with 16-bit values are always 3 bytes, with the 16-bit value stored low byte first; this little-endian order is shared by the 8086.

formulas.title: 8086 effective address
formulas.description: General form for memory operands; base is BX or BP, index is SI or DI, and each term is optional.

formulas.title: Physical address of a data operand
formulas.plainText: PA = DS × 10H + EA (SS instead of DS when BP is used)
formulas.description: Combine the effective address with the default segment to get the 20-bit address the BIU drives onto the bus.

formulas.title: 8085 instruction length
formulas.plainText: L = 1 + number of operand bytes (0, 1 or 2)
formulas.description: Register and indirect instructions are 1 byte, 8-bit immediate or port instructions 2 bytes, 16-bit address or data instructions 3 bytes.

flashcards.front: Name the five 8085 addressing modes with one example each.
flashcards.back: Immediate (MVI A, 25H), register (MOV A, B), direct (LDA 2050H), register indirect (MOV A, M using HL), implicit (CMA).

flashcards.front: Which segment does the 8086 use for MOV AX, [BP+6], and why?
flashcards.back: The stack segment SS, because any address using BP defaults to SS; BP exists to reach parameters and local variables on the stack.

flashcards.front: With BX = 0100H, DI = 0020H and DS = 1000H, what physical address does MOV AL, [BX+DI+5] access?
flashcards.back: EA = 0100H + 0020H + 0005H = 0125H; PA = 10000H + 0125H = 10125H. The mode is based-indexed with displacement.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between MOV AX, [SI] and MOV AX, [SI+4]?
flashcards.back: MOV AX, [SI] is register indirect (EA = SI). MOV AX, [SI+4] is indexed addressing (EA = SI + 4); the added constant is the displacement.

questions.questionText: In an 8086 system DS = 1000H, BX = 2000H and SI = 0100H. The physical address accessed by MOV AX, [BX+SI+04H] is:
questions.explanation: EA = BX + SI + displacement = 2000H + 0100H + 0004H = 2104H. PA = DS × 10H + EA = 10000H + 2104H = 12104H. The mode is based-indexed with displacement and uses DS because the base is BX.

questions.questionText: In the 8085 instruction MVI B, 3AH, the value 3AH is specified using which addressing mode?
questions.explanation: The data byte 3AH is part of the instruction itself (second byte of MVI), which is immediate addressing.

questions.questionText: The 8085 instruction LDAX D loads the accumulator using which addressing mode?
questions.explanation: LDAX D reads the memory location whose address is held in the DE pair, so the register pair points to the operand: register indirect addressing.

questions.questionText: Which addressing mode is used by the 8085 instruction STA 3000H?
questions.explanation: The 16-bit memory address 3000H is written in the instruction, so the operand location is given directly.

questions.questionText: The 8085 instruction CMA (complement accumulator) uses which addressing mode?
questions.explanation: CMA has no operand field; the opcode itself says the accumulator is complemented, which is implied addressing.

questions.questionText: According to the standard classification, how many addressing modes does the 8085 support?
questions.explanation: The 8085 has five modes: immediate, register, direct, register indirect and implied. The 8086 has a larger set of modes.

questions.questionText: Which 8086 addressing mode does MOV AX, [SI+08H] use for its source operand?
questions.explanation: An index register (SI or DI) plus a displacement is indexed addressing (also called register relative); based addressing uses BX or BP.

questions.questionText: Which 8086 addressing mode is used by the source operand of MOV AX, [BX+SI+05H]?
questions.explanation: The address combines a base register (BX), an index register (SI) and a displacement (05H), which is based-indexed with displacement.

questions.questionText: In the 8086 instruction MOV AL, [2000H], the source operand is accessed using:
questions.explanation: The brackets around a constant mean the constant is a memory offset (EA = 2000H in DS), which is direct addressing; without brackets 2000H would be immediate data.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is NOT a valid 8086 memory operand?
questions.explanation: In 16-bit 8086 addressing only BX and BP (base) and SI and DI (index) may appear inside brackets; AX cannot be used as a pointer.

questions.questionText: For the 8086 string instruction MOVSB, the source and destination bytes are located at:
questions.explanation: String instructions read the source through DS:SI and write the destination through ES:DI, then adjust SI and DI according to DF.

questions.questionText: The 8086 instruction JNZ NEXT locates its target address using which addressing mode?
questions.explanation: Conditional jumps carry only a signed 8-bit displacement that is added to IP of the next instruction, so they use relative addressing.

questions.questionText: Which addressing mode gives the fastest operand access because the operand is already inside the CPU and no memory bus cycle is required for it?
questions.explanation: In register mode both operands are in CPU registers, so no memory read or address calculation is needed; all memory modes need at least one bus cycle.

questions.questionText: The 8086 instruction IN AL, DX addresses the input port using:
options: Variable (indirect) port addressing with the port number in DX, allowing ports 0000H–FFFFH
Fixed port addressing with ports 00H–FFH only
Immediate addressing with a 16-bit port number in the instruction
questions.explanation: When the port number is in DX the instruction can reach any of 65,536 ports; the fixed form IN AL, 80H carries an 8-bit port number and reaches only 00H–FFH.

questions.questionText: The 8085 instruction LXI B, 4523H is stored in memory starting at address 2000H. What is the byte at address 2001H?
questions.explanation: LXI B is 3 bytes: opcode 01H at 2000H, then the 16-bit data low byte first, so 2001H holds 23H and 2002H holds 45H.

questions.questionText: In an 8086 system DS = 3000H and BX = 0500H. What physical address is read by MOV AL, [BX+25H]?
In an 8086 system DS = 2000H, SS = 4000H and BP = 0200H. What physical address is read by MOV AX, [BP+10H]?
questions.explanation: EA = BP + 10H = 0210H. Because BP is used, the default segment is SS: PA = 40000H + 0210H = 40210H.

questions.questionText: In an 8086 system DS = 1200H and SI = 0034H. What physical address is read by MOV CL, [SI+0100H]?
In an 8086 system DS = 2100H, BX = 0150H and DI = 0020H. At which physical address does MOV [BX+DI], AL store AL?
In an 8086 system DS = 2000H, SS = 5000H, BP = 0300H and SI = 0040H. From which physical address does MOV DX, [BP+SI+06H] read its low byte?
questions.explanation: EA = 0300H + 0040H + 06H = 0346H. The operand contains BP, so SS is the default segment: PA = 50000H + 0346H = 50346H (DL comes from here, DH from 50347H).

questions.questionText: In an 8086 system DS = 1000H, ES = 6000H and BX = 0010H. Which physical address is read by MOV AX, ES:[BX+02H]?
questions.explanation: The ES: override replaces the default DS. EA = 0010H + 02H = 0012H; PA = 60000H + 0012H = 60012H.

questions.questionText: In an 8086 system DS = 1000H, memory location 10300H contains 34H and 10301H contains 12H. What is AX after MOV AX, [0300H]?
questions.explanation: Direct addressing: EA = 0300H, PA = 10300H. A word is stored low byte first, so AL = 34H (from 10300H), AH = 12H (from 10301H) and AX = 1234H.

questions.questionText: In an 8086 system DS = 2000H, BX = FFF0H and SI = 0020H. Which physical address is read by MOV AL, [BX+SI]?
questions.explanation: EA = FFF0H + 0020H = 10010H, but the EA is only 16 bits, so it wraps to 0010H. PA = 20000H + 0010H = 20010H; the carry does not spill into the next segment.

questions.questionText: On the 8086, CS = 1000H, DS = 2000H and BX = 0300H. Memory locations 20300H and 20301H hold 50H and 04H. The near jump JMP WORD PTR [BX] is executed. From which physical address is the next instruction fetched?
questions.explanation: This is memory-indirect program addressing: the pointer is read from DS:BX = 20000H + 0300H = 20300H, and the little-endian word there, 0450H, is loaded into IP. CS is unchanged, so the next fetch is at 1000H × 10H + 0450H = 10450H.

questions.questionText: In an 8086 system DS = 2500H. What value must BX hold so that MOV AL, [BX] reads physical address 26A40H?
questions.explanation: EA = PA − DS × 10H = 26A40H − 25000H = 1A40H, so BX = 1A40H.

questions.questionText: An 8086 instruction MOV AX, [BX+SI+00C0H] reads physical address 3A2F4H with BX = 1200H and SI = 0034H. What is the value in DS?
On the 8086, DF = 0, DS = 1000H, ES = 2000H, SI = 0100H and DI = 0200H. After one MOVSB, which physical address was written and what are SI and DI?
questions.explanation: The destination is ES:DI = 20000H + 0200H = 20200H. With DF = 0 a byte transfer increments SI and DI by 1, giving 0101H and 0201H.

questions.questionText: On the 8086, DF = 1, SI = 0300H and DI = 0500H. What are SI and DI after one MOVSW?
questions.explanation: DF = 1 means auto-decrement, and a word transfer moves the pointers by 2: SI = 0300H − 2 = 02FEH, DI = 0500H − 2 = 04FEH.

questions.questionText: On the 8086, DF = 0, CX = 0005H, SI = 0200H and DI = 0400H. What are CX, SI and DI after REP MOVSB finishes?
questions.explanation: REP repeats MOVSB while CX ≠ 0: five bytes are moved, each move adds 1 to SI and DI and subtracts 1 from CX, so CX = 0, SI = 0205H, DI = 0405H.

questions.questionText: On the 8086, SS = 3000H, BP = 1000H and SI = 0200H. What does BX contain after LEA BX, [BP+SI+20H]?
questions.explanation: LEA loads the effective address itself, not the memory contents and not the physical address: BX = 1000H + 0200H + 20H = 1220H.

questions.questionText: On the 8086, DS = 1000H, BX = 0300H and AL = 05H. From which physical address does XLAT read the byte that replaces AL?
questions.explanation: XLAT uses EA = BX + AL = 0300H + 05H = 0305H in DS: PA = 10000H + 0305H = 10305H.

questions.questionText: A 2-byte 8086 instruction JMP SHORT L1 is located at CS:0100H and its displacement byte is 10H. What is the offset of L1?
questions.explanation: IP already points to the next instruction, 0100H + 2 = 0102H. Target = 0102H + 10H = 0112H.

questions.questionText: A 2-byte 8086 instruction JNZ BACK is located at CS:0200H with displacement byte F6H, and ZF = 0. What is IP after it executes?
questions.explanation: F6H as a signed byte is −10 (−0AH). IP of the next instruction = 0202H, so the target is 0202H − 000AH = 01F8H. The jump is taken because ZF = 0.

questions.questionText: An 8086 JMP SHORT instruction (2 bytes) is placed at offset 0150H and must jump back to offset 0130H. What displacement byte is encoded?
questions.explanation: d = target − (address + length) = 0130H − 0152H = −22H. In 8-bit two's complement −22H = 100H − 22H = DEH.

questions.questionText: In an 8085 system memory location 2500H holds 34H and 2501H holds 12H. What are H and L after LHLD 2500H?
questions.explanation: LHLD uses direct addressing: L is loaded from 2500H (34H) and H from the next address 2501H (12H), so HL = 1234H.

questions.questionText: An 8085 has B = 20H and C = 30H. Memory location 2030H holds 7FH and 3020H holds 11H. What is in the accumulator after LDAX B?
questions.explanation: LDAX B uses BC as a pointer with B as the high byte: address = 2030H, so A = 7FH.

questions.questionText: How many bytes of memory does this 8085 program occupy? LXI H, 2050H / MVI M, 0AH / LDA 2051H / ADD M / OUT 01H / HLT
questions.explanation: LXI (3) + MVI M (2) + LDA (3) + ADD M (1) + OUT (2) + HLT (1) = 12 bytes. Immediate 8-bit data and port numbers add one byte, 16-bit addresses or data add two.

questions.questionText: On the 8086, SS = 3000H and SP = 0200H. When PUSH BX executes, at which physical address is the byte BH stored?
questions.explanation: PUSH makes SP = 0200H − 2 = 01FEH and stores the word at SS:SP low byte first: BL at 301FEH and BH at 301FFH.

questions.questionText: Which of the following 8086 memory operands is illegal?
questions.explanation: An 8086 address may contain at most one base register (BX or BP) and one index register (SI or DI); BX and BP are both base registers.

questions.questionText: Which statement about 8086 segment override prefixes is correct?
options: An override prefix stays in effect for all following instructions until another prefix appears
Operands that use BP can never be taken from any segment other than SS
The ES:DI destination of a string instruction cannot be overridden
The segment used by PUSH and POP can be changed with an ES: prefix
questions.explanation: A prefix affects only the one instruction it precedes; BP operands can be overridden (for example DS:[BP]); stack operations always use SS, and the string destination is always ES:DI.

questions.questionText: The 8086 assembler rejects the instruction MOV [BX], 25H. Why?
options: Immediate data cannot be moved into memory
BX cannot be used as a memory pointer
The operand size is unknown; BYTE PTR or WORD PTR must be given
questions.explanation: Neither [BX] nor 25H fixes whether a byte or a word is meant, so the programmer must write MOV BYTE PTR [BX], 25H or MOV WORD PTR [BX], 25H. Immediate-to-memory moves are legal.

questions.questionText: Which addressing mode is NOT available on the 8085?
questions.explanation: The 8085 has no index registers and cannot add a displacement to a pointer; its five modes are immediate, register, direct, register indirect and implied.

questions.questionText: In an 8086 system DS = 1000H, SS = 2000H, BX = 0100H, BP = 0100H and SI = 0010H. Which instruction reads physical address 20110H?
questions.explanation: All four have EA = 0110H. Only [BP+SI] without an override uses SS (20000H + 0110H = 20110H); the others use DS and read 10110H.

questions.questionText: In an 8086 system DS = 4000H and BX = 0100H. Which physical address is read by MOV AL, [BX-02H]?
questions.explanation: The displacement −2 is stored as FEH and sign-extended to FFFEH. EA = 0100H − 2 = 00FEH; PA = 40000H + 00FEH = 400FEH.

questions.questionText: On the 8086, a word array MAT starts at offset 0400H with 10 words per row (row-major, zero-based) and DS = 2000H. MAT[2][3] is read by MOV AX, [BX+SI+0400H] with BX = row × bytes per row and SI = column × 2. What physical address is read?
On the 8086, a word array ARR starts at offset 0200H. To read element number 5 (zero-based) with MOV AX, [SI+0200H], what value must SI hold?
questions.explanation: Each word occupies 2 bytes, so the byte offset of element 5 is 5 × 2 = 10 = 000AH; the base 0200H is already in the displacement.

questions.questionText: In the 8086 instruction MOV AL, [BX+disp8], how is the 8-bit displacement used when forming the effective address?
options: It is zero-extended to 16 bits and added to BX
It is sign-extended to 16 bits and added to BX
It is added to the segment register before the shift
It is multiplied by 16 and added to the physical address
questions.explanation: An 8-bit displacement (mod = 01) is treated as a signed value from −128 to +127 and sign-extended before the 16-bit addition, which is why [BX-2] can be encoded in one displacement byte.

concepts.text: Data transfer details that MCQs test:
items: MOV dest, src copies without changing flags. Illegal forms: memory to memory, segment register to segment register, immediate to a segment register, and CS as destination; go through a register (MOV AX, DATA then MOV DS, AX).
PUSH src decrements SP by 2 then stores a word; POP dest loads a word then increments SP by 2. PUSHF/POPF save and restore the flag register.
LEA reg, mem loads the offset (effective address) of a variable, not its contents; MOV reg, mem loads the contents.
IN AL, port / IN AX, port and OUT port, AL use an 8-bit port number in the instruction or a 16-bit port number in DX; the data is always in AL or AX.

concepts.text: Arithmetic and logical details:
items: ADD, ADC (add with carry), SUB, SBB (subtract with borrow) and NEG update CF, PF, AF, ZF, SF and OF. INC and DEC update all of these except CF, so a loop counter can be decremented without disturbing a carry.
CMP a, b computes a − b, sets the flags and discards the result; it is always followed by a conditional jump. TEST a, b does the same with AND.
AND masks bits, OR sets bits, XOR toggles bits and XOR AX, AX is the standard way to clear a register; NOT complements every bit and affects no flags.
Shifts and rotates take a count of 1 or the value in CL; SHL doubles, SHR halves an unsigned number, SAR preserves the sign bit.

concepts.text: Control transfer:
items: JMP target is unconditional (short: 8-bit displacement, near: 16-bit within the segment, far: new CS:IP). Conditional jumps are always short (−128 to +127 bytes).
Unsigned comparisons use JA, JAE, JB, JBE (above/below, from CF and ZF); signed comparisons use JG, JGE, JL, JLE (greater/less, from SF, OF and ZF). JE/JZ and JNE/JNZ are the same opcodes.
CALL pushes the return address (IP for near, CS then IP for far) and jumps; RET pops it back. RET n additionally discards n bytes of parameters from the stack.
LOOP label decrements CX and jumps while CX ≠ 0; LOOPE/LOOPZ and LOOPNE/LOOPNZ also test ZF. INT n pushes flags, CS and IP and jumps through the vector at 4n; IRET pops them all back.

concepts.text: String instructions work on a byte (B suffix) or word (W suffix) at DS:SI and/or ES:DI, then move SI and DI automatically:
items: MOVSB/MOVSW copies DS:[SI] to ES:[DI]; CMPSB compares them; SCASB compares AL with ES:[DI]; LODSB loads AL from DS:[SI]; STOSB stores AL at ES:[DI].
DF = 0 (CLD) increments SI and DI by 1 or 2; DF = 1 (STD) decrements them.
REP repeats the instruction CX times (CX decremented each pass); REPE/REPZ repeats while equal, REPNE/REPNZ while not equal, for CMPS and SCAS. Set CX, SI, DI and DF before every string operation.

concepts.text: Assembler Directives and Program Structure

Each source line has the form [Label:] Mnemonic [Operands] [; Comment]. A label names an address and must start with a letter or underscore; the assembler replaces it with an offset. Instructions become machine code; directives (pseudo-ops) do not: they tell the assembler how to reserve storage, define constants, split the program into segments and mark where it begins and ends. Numbers ending in H are hexadecimal and must start with a digit (0FFH, not FFH); B marks binary and a bare number is decimal.

rows: Define byte / word / doubleword storage, optionally initialised
ARR DB 10H, 20H, 30H ; SUM DW ? ; MSG DB 'HELLO$'
Give a constant a name (no storage)
Begin and end a logical segment
Tell the assembler which segment register addresses which segment
Begin and end a procedure (NEAR or FAR)
End of source; optional entry label

concepts.text: Example Program: Sum of a Byte Array

DATA SEGMENT
    ARR  DB 10H, 20H, 30H, 40H, 50H   ; five bytes
    SUM  DW ?                         ; 16-bit result
DATA ENDS

CODE SEGMENT
    ASSUME CS:CODE, DS:DATA
START:
    MOV AX, DATA
    MOV DS, AX          ; initialise data segment
    LEA SI, ARR         ; SI -> first element
    MOV CX, 05H         ; element count
    XOR AX, AX          ; AX = 0, running sum
NEXT:
    MOV BL, [SI]        ; fetch one byte
    MOV BH, 00H         ; zero-extend to 16 bits
    ADD AX, BX          ; accumulate
    INC SI              ; point to next byte
    LOOP NEXT           ; CX = CX - 1, repeat while CX != 0
    MOV SUM, AX         ; store result (00F0H)
    MOV AH, 4CH
    INT 21H             ; return to DOS
CODE ENDS
END START
Step by step:
items: DS cannot be loaded with an immediate, so the segment address DATA goes through AX first.
LEA SI, ARR puts the offset of the array in SI (register indirect access follows); MOV CX, 05H sets the loop count and XOR AX, AX clears the accumulator.
Inside the loop a byte is read via [SI], widened to a word in BX and added to AX, so the sum can exceed 255 without losing a carry; INC SI advances the pointer.
LOOP NEXT is DEC CX followed by JNZ NEXT; after five passes CX = 0 and execution falls through to store 10H + 20H + 30H + 40H + 50H = 00F0H in SUM.
Function 4CH of INT 21H terminates the program; without it the CPU would execute whatever follows in memory.

concepts.text: The stack lives in the stack segment and grows downward: SP starts at the top and every PUSH stores a word at SS:SP − 2. CALL pushes the return address, the procedure (defined between PROC and ENDP) runs, and RET pops the address back into IP (and CS for a FAR procedure). Registers a procedure uses should be pushed at entry and popped in reverse order before RET; an unbalanced stack sends RET to a wrong address. Parameters are passed in registers or on the stack and read through BP.

rows: CALL name; body stored once, executed via CALL/RET
Name written like an instruction; assembler pastes the body at each use
Via registers, memory or the stack

Short sequences used a few times

concepts.text: DAA corrects the accumulator after adding two packed BCD bytes. It looks at the lower nibble first: if that nibble is above 9 or AC = 1, it adds 06H. It then looks at the upper nibble: if that nibble is above 9 or CY = 1, it adds 60H and sets CY. On the 8085, DAA is valid only after an addition; the 8086 adds DAS for BCD subtraction.

Worked example 1: BCD addition with DAA (8085)
  47H + 38H = 7FH        AC = 0, CY = 0
  low nibble F > 9   -> add 06H -> 85H
  high nibble 8 <= 9 and CY = 0 -> no change
  A = 85H, CY = 0        (47 + 38 = 85 in decimal)

  75H + 48H = BDH        AC = 0, CY = 0
  low nibble D > 9   -> add 06H -> C3H
  high nibble C > 9  -> add 60H -> 123H
  A = 23H, CY = 1        (75 + 48 = 123 in decimal)

LOOP:   DCR B          ; 4T, 50 times

concepts.text: Common mistakes in instruction-result questions:
items: Expecting DCX or INX to set Z; they change no flags, so a 16-bit counter needs MOV A, D / ORA E before JNZ.
Counting 10T for every JNZ; the final, not-taken JNZ takes 7T.
Treating a count of 00H as zero passes; DCR from 00H gives FFH, so the loop runs 256 times.
Forgetting that ANA sets AC on the 8085 and that ANA, ORA and XRA always clear CY.
Popping registers in the same order they were pushed; the stack is last-in, first-out.
Confusing RLC (bit 7 goes to bit 0 and CY) with RAL (old CY goes to bit 0).

concepts.text: For a short program, draw a table with one row per instruction and columns for every register, flag and memory location it touches. Fill each row from the one above; most result questions are then pure bookkeeping.
CMP behaves like SUB for the flags but leaves the accumulator unchanged. After CMP, CY = 1 means the accumulator was smaller (unsigned), which is the opposite of what many students first guess.

formulas.plainText: LOOP label = DEC CX + JNZ label (flags not changed by LOOP itself)
PUSH: SP = SP − 2; POP: SP = SP + 2
MUL r16: DX:AX = AX × r16 (32-bit product); MUL r8: AX = AL × r8

formulas.latex: \text{DIV } r8:\ AL \leftarrow \lfloor AX / r8 \rfloor,\ AH \leftarrow AX \bmod r8
formulas.plainText: DIV r8: AL = AX ÷ r8 (quotient), AH = remainder; DIV r16: AX = DX:AX ÷ r16, DX = remainder

notes.text: MUL BL puts the product in AX; MUL BX puts it in DX:AX. DIV BL leaves the quotient in AL and the remainder in AH; DIV BX leaves them in AX and DX. Where the result lands is a repeat question.
MOV [SI], [DI], MOV DS, 1000H and MOV DS, ES are all illegal on the 8086. Also remember INC and DEC do not touch CF, so a carry from an earlier ADD survives a counter update.
Directives (DB, DW, EQU, ORG, ASSUME, END) generate no machine code; EQU in particular reserves no memory, whereas DB and DW do.

formulas.title: LOOP equivalence
formulas.plainText: LOOP L = DEC CX ; JNZ L
formulas.description: LOOP decrements CX and branches while it is non-zero, so a loop set up with MOV CX, n runs n times.

formulas.title: Stack pointer on PUSH and POP
formulas.description: Each stack operation moves a 16-bit word, so SP changes by 2; the stack grows toward lower addresses.

formulas.title: MUL result registers
formulas.latex: AX = AL \times r8,\qquad DX{:}AX = AX \times r16
formulas.plainText: MUL r8: AX = AL × r8; MUL r16: DX:AX = AX × r16
formulas.description: Unsigned multiply always uses the accumulator as the implied operand and doubles the width of the result.

formulas.title: DIV result registers
formulas.latex: AL = \lfloor AX / r8 \rfloor,\ AH = AX \bmod r8
formulas.plainText: DIV r8: AL = quotient, AH = remainder (DIV r16: AX quotient, DX remainder)
formulas.description: Unsigned divide of the double-width accumulator; a quotient that does not fit causes a type-0 (divide error) interrupt.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between CMP AX, BX and SUB AX, BX?
flashcards.back: Both compute AX − BX and set the flags, but CMP discards the result while SUB stores it in AX. CMP is used before a conditional jump.

flashcards.front: Which directives reserve memory and which do not?
flashcards.back: DB, DW and DD reserve (and may initialise) bytes, words and doublewords. EQU, ORG, ASSUME, SEGMENT/ENDS, PROC/ENDP and END generate no code and reserve no memory.

flashcards.front: What does CALL push on the stack, and what does RET do?
flashcards.back: A near CALL pushes IP (return offset); a far CALL pushes CS then IP. RET pops them back so execution resumes after the CALL; RET n also discards n bytes of parameters.

flashcards.front: Compare a macro with a procedure.
flashcards.back: A macro is expanded in place by the assembler at every use (faster, larger code); a procedure is stored once and reached by CALL/RET (smaller code, call overhead).

questions.questionText: In an 8086 program AX = 0025H and BL = 04H. After DIV BL is executed, the registers contain:
questions.explanation: 0025H = 37 decimal; 37 ÷ 4 = 9 remainder 1. For an 8-bit divisor the quotient goes to AL (09H) and the remainder to AH (01H).

questions.questionText: Which flag is NOT affected by the 8086 instruction INC AX?
questions.explanation: INC and DEC update PF, AF, ZF, SF and OF but deliberately leave the carry flag unchanged, so a counter can be updated without destroying a carry from a previous addition.

questions.questionText: If SP = 1000H before PUSH AX is executed on the 8086, the value of SP afterwards is:
questions.explanation: PUSH first decrements SP by 2 (one 16-bit word) and then stores AX at SS:SP, so SP becomes 1000H − 2 = 0FFEH. The stack grows toward lower addresses.

questions.questionText: On the 8085, A = 6CH and CY = 1. What is the result of XRA A?
questions.explanation: Any value XORed with itself is 0, so A = 00H and Z = 1; XRA always clears CY (and AC). XRA A is a common one-byte way to clear A and CY together.

questions.questionText: Which of these 8085 instructions affects no flags at all?
questions.explanation: The 16-bit increment and decrement instructions INX and DCX change no flags. INR changes S, Z, AC and P; ADD and CMP change all five.

questions.questionText: On the 8085, A = 25H and B = 40H. What are CY and Z after CMP B?
questions.explanation: CMP computes A − B = 25H − 40H without storing it. A is smaller, so a borrow occurs (CY = 1) and the result is not zero (Z = 0).

questions.questionText: What is the effect of the 8086 instruction CLD?
options: DF = 1, so string instructions auto-decrement SI and DI
DF = 0, so string instructions auto-increment SI and DI
questions.explanation: CLD clears the direction flag; with DF = 0 string instructions move SI and DI upward. STD sets DF, CLC clears CF and CLI clears IF.

questions.questionText: Which 8085 machine-control instruction sets the masks for RST 7.5, 6.5 and 5.5 and can send a bit out on the SOD line?
questions.explanation: SIM (set interrupt mask) takes its control byte from the accumulator for the masks and the serial output bit; RIM reads the masks, pending interrupts and SID back into A.

questions.questionText: Which registers does the 8085 instruction PUSH PSW save on the stack?
options: The accumulator and the flag register
questions.explanation: PSW (program status word) is the 16-bit pair formed by A (high byte) and the flag register (low byte).

questions.questionText: The 8085 instruction JPE LABEL transfers control when:
questions.explanation: JPE means jump on parity even, taken when the parity flag is set; JPO is taken when P = 0.

questions.questionText: In 8086 assembly language, how many bytes of memory does the data definition BUF DW 8 DUP(0) reserve?
questions.explanation: DW defines 2-byte words and 8 DUP(0) repeats the initial value 0 eight times, so 8 × 2 = 16 bytes are reserved. DB would reserve 8 bytes and DD 32 bytes.

questions.questionText: What is the carry flag after the 8085 executes STC followed by CMC?
options: CY keeps the value it had before STC
questions.explanation: STC sets CY to 1 and CMC complements it, giving CY = 0. Neither instruction touches Z.

questions.questionText: Which of these 8086 instructions changes no flags?
questions.explanation: Data-transfer instructions such as MOV leave FLAGS alone; CMP, TEST and NEG all update the status flags.

questions.questionText: What does the 8086 instruction TEST AL, 01H do?
options: It ANDs AL with 01H and stores the result in AL
It subtracts 01H from AL and sets the flags
It ANDs AL with 01H, sets the flags and discards the result
It sets bit 0 of AL to 1
questions.explanation: TEST is a non-destructive AND: the flags (ZF in particular) show whether bit 0 is set, while AL is unchanged. It clears CF and OF.

questions.questionText: When the 8085 executes RET, the stack pointer:
questions.explanation: RET pops the 16-bit return address into PC, reading two bytes and adding 2 to SP.

questions.questionText: What does the 8085 instruction DAD B do?
options: Adds BC to HL and updates all five flags
Adds B to A and applies decimal adjustment
Adds BC to HL, leaves the sum in HL and affects only CY
questions.explanation: DAD rp is a 16-bit addition HL = HL + rp. Only the carry flag reports an overflow out of bit 15.

questions.questionText: On the 8085, A = 5AH. What is A after XRI 0FFH?
questions.explanation: XOR with 1 inverts a bit, so XOR with FFH complements every bit: 0101 1010 becomes 1010 0101 = A5H.

questions.questionText: On the 8085, A = 85H and CY = 0. What are A and CY after RLC?
questions.explanation: 85H = 1000 0101. RLC moves bit 7 into both bit 0 and CY: 0000 1011 = 0BH, CY = 1.

questions.questionText: On the 8085, A = 85H and CY = 0. What are A and CY after RAL?
questions.explanation: RAL rotates through carry: bit 7 (1) goes to CY and the old CY (0) enters bit 0, so 1000 0101 becomes 0000 1010 = 0AH with CY = 1.

questions.questionText: On the 8085, A = 37H and B = 5AH. What are A and CY after SUB B?
questions.explanation: 37H − 5AH = −23H, stored as the two's complement 100H − 23H = DDH. A borrow was needed, so CY = 1 (and S = 1).

questions.questionText: What are A and CY after this 8085 sequence? MVI A, 38H / MVI B, 45H / ADD B / DAA
questions.explanation: 38H + 45H = 7DH. The low nibble D is above 9, so DAA adds 06H giving 83H; the high nibble 8 needs no correction. BCD check: 38 + 45 = 83.

questions.questionText: On the 8085, A = C5H, B = 3CH and CY = 1. What are A, CY and AC after ANA B?
questions.explanation: 1100 0101 AND 0011 1100 = 0000 0100 = 04H. On the 8085, ANA always clears CY and sets AC.

questions.questionText: On the 8085, HL = 8000H and BC = 9000H. What are HL and CY after DAD B?
questions.explanation: 8000H + 9000H = 11000H. Only 16 bits fit in HL, so HL = 1000H and the carry out of bit 15 sets CY.

questions.questionText: On the 8085, SP = 2100H. After LXI B, 1234H and PUSH B, what are the byte at 20FFH and SP?
questions.explanation: PUSH B decrements SP and stores B (12H) at 20FFH, decrements again and stores C (34H) at 20FEH; SP ends at 20FEH.

questions.questionText: An 8085 program starts at 2000H: LXI H, 2050H / MVI C, 0AH / L: MOV A, M ... At which address is the label L?
questions.explanation: LXI H occupies 2000H–2002H (3 bytes) and MVI C occupies 2003H–2004H (2 bytes), so MOV A, M starts at 2005H.

questions.questionText: On the 8085, [2050H] = 49H and [2051H] = 6AH. What is stored at 2052H after LDA 2050H / MOV B, A / LDA 2051H / ADD B / STA 2052H?
questions.explanation: 49H + 6AH: 9 + A = 13H (write 3, carry 1), 4 + 6 + 1 = B, so the sum is B3H, which STA stores at 2052H.

questions.questionText: What is in A when this 8085 program halts? MVI A, 00H / MVI B, 05H / MVI C, 03H / L: ADD B / DCR C / JNZ L / HLT
questions.explanation: The loop runs C = 3 times, adding B = 5 each time: A = 5 × 3 = 15 = 0FH. This is multiplication by repeated addition.

questions.questionText: How many times does the body of this 8085 loop execute? MVI C, 00H / L: DCR C / JNZ L
questions.explanation: The first DCR turns 00H into FFH (not zero), so the loop continues; Z becomes 1 only after C has counted FFH down to 00H, a total of 256 passes.

questions.questionText: An 8085 programmer writes LXI B, 0005H / L: DCX B / JNZ L as a counted loop. What is wrong with it?
options: DCX B decrements only register C, so B is never tested
DCX does not affect the Z flag, so JNZ tests a stale flag; MOV A, C / ORA B is needed before JNZ
JNZ cannot be used after a 16-bit instruction
LXI B loads the count into B and C in the wrong order
questions.explanation: INX and DCX change no flags, so JNZ keeps using whatever Z was set earlier. ORing the two halves of the pair sets Z only when BC = 0000H.

questions.questionText: What is AX after this 8086 code? MOV CX, 5 / MOV AX, 0 / L: ADD AX, CX / LOOP L
questions.explanation: LOOP decrements CX and repeats while CX ≠ 0, so AX = 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 15 = 000FH.

questions.questionText: On the 8086, AL = B4H. What are AL and CF after SHL AL, 1?
questions.explanation: 1011 0100 shifted left gives 0110 1000 = 68H; the bit shifted out of bit 7 (1) goes to CF and a 0 enters bit 0.

questions.questionText: On the 8086, AL = F0H. What are AL and CF after SAR AL, 1?
questions.explanation: SAR shifts right but copies the sign bit into bit 7: 1111 0000 becomes 1111 1000 = F8H (−16 ÷ 2 = −8), and bit 0 (0) goes to CF. SHR would give 78H.

questions.questionText: What is AL after this 8086 sequence? MOV AL, 0F0H / AND AL, 3CH / OR AL, 01H / XOR AL, 0FFH
questions.explanation: F0H AND 3CH = 30H; 30H OR 01H = 31H; 31H XOR FFH = CEH (every bit inverted).

questions.questionText: On the 8086, AX = 1111H and BX = 2222H. What are AX and BX after PUSH AX / PUSH BX / POP AX / POP BX?
questions.explanation: The stack is last-in, first-out: POP AX takes the last value pushed (BX = 2222H) and POP BX takes 1111H, so the registers are swapped.

questions.questionText: An 8086 near procedure ends with RET 4. If SP = 0FF0H just before RET 4 executes, what is SP afterwards?
questions.explanation: RET pops the 2-byte return offset (SP + 2) and then adds the 4 parameter bytes: 0FF0H + 2 + 4 = 0FF6H.

questions.questionText: The 8086 instruction LOOPE (LOOPZ) label jumps back to label when, after CX is decremented:
options: CX ≠ 0, whatever the value of ZF
questions.explanation: LOOPE continues while the count is not exhausted and the last comparison was equal; LOOPNE needs ZF = 0, and plain LOOP ignores ZF.

questions.questionText: Which statement about 8086 CALL and RET is NOT correct?
options: A near CALL pushes only IP
A far CALL pushes CS and then IP
RET 6 adds 6 to SP after popping the return address
A near RET pops both IP and CS from the stack
questions.explanation: A near return pops only IP (2 bytes); popping both IP and CS (4 bytes) is what a far RET does.

questions.questionText: On the 8086, AL = 70H and BL = 30H. What are OF and CF after ADD AL, BL?
questions.explanation: 70H + 30H = A0H. No carry leaves bit 7 (CF = 0), but two positive signed numbers (+112 and +48) gave a negative-looking result, so OF = 1.

questions.questionText: On the 8085, HL = 1234H, DE = 5678H and SP = 2000H, and memory locations 2000H and 2001H hold 9AH and BCH. What are HL and DE after XCHG followed by XTHL?
questions.explanation: XCHG swaps HL and DE, giving HL = 5678H and DE = 1234H. XTHL then exchanges L with [SP] and H with [SP + 1], so L = 9AH and H = BCH (HL = BC9AH), while 2000H and 2001H receive 78H and 56H and SP stays 2000H.

questions.questionText: On the 8085, A = 9AH and B = 89H. What are A, CY, AC and P after ADD B?
questions.explanation: 9AH + 89H = 123H, so A = 23H and CY = 1. Low nibbles A + 9 = 19 > 15 gives AC = 1. 23H = 0010 0011 has three 1s (odd), so P = 0.

questions.questionText: What are A and CY after this 8085 sequence? MVI A, 99H / ADI 01H / DAA
questions.explanation: 99H + 01H = 9AH. The low nibble A > 9, so DAA adds 06H: A0H. The high nibble A > 9, so it adds 60H: 100H, leaving A = 00H with CY = 1. BCD check: 99 + 1 = 100.

questions.questionText: On the 8085, SP = 2400H. After LXI B, 1234H / PUSH B / POP PSW, what are the accumulator and the flag register?
questions.explanation: PUSH B stores B (12H) at 23FFH and C (34H) at 23FEH. POP PSW loads the flag register from [SP] = 34H and A from [SP + 1] = 12H.

questions.questionText: On the 8085, SP = 2400H and the 3-byte instruction CALL 3000H is stored at 2000H. After the CALL executes, what are [23FFH], [23FEH] and SP?
questions.explanation: The return address is the next instruction, 2000H + 3 = 2003H. CALL pushes its high byte 20H at 23FFH and low byte 03H at 23FEH, so SP = 23FEH and PC = 3000H.

questions.questionText: How many T-states does this 8085 delay segment take? MVI C, 0FFH (7T) / L: DCR C (4T) / JNZ L (10T if taken, 7T if not)
questions.explanation: FFH = 255 passes of 4T + 10T = 3570T, plus 7T for MVI, minus 3T because the last JNZ is not taken: 7 + 255 × 14 − 3 = 3574 T-states.

questions.questionText: An 8085 runs at 3 MHz. What delay does this segment produce? LXI D, 03E8H (10T) / L: DCX D (6T) / MOV A, D (4T) / ORA E (4T) / JNZ L (10T taken, 7T not taken)
questions.explanation: 03E8H = 1000 passes of 6 + 4 + 4 + 10 = 24T. T = 10 + 1000 × 24 − 3 = 24,007 T-states; at 3 MHz one T-state is 0.333 µs, so the delay is 24,007 ÷ 3 MHz ≈ 8.00 ms.

questions.questionText: On the 8086, AL = 80H and BL = 01H. After CMP AL, BL, which of the conditional jumps JA and JG is taken?
options: Both JA and JG are taken
JG is taken but JA is not taken
Neither JA nor JG is taken
JA is taken but JG is not taken
questions.explanation: Unsigned, 80H = 128 > 1, so CF = 0 and ZF = 0 and JA is taken. Signed, 80H = −128 < +1: 80H − 01H = 7FH gives SF = 0 and OF = 1, SF ≠ OF, so JG is not taken.

questions.questionText: On the 8086, AL = FFH and BL = 02H. What does AX contain after MUL BL, and what would it contain after IMUL BL instead?
questions.explanation: MUL treats FFH as 255: 255 × 2 = 510 = 01FEH. IMUL treats FFH as −1: −1 × 2 = −2, which is FFFEH as a 16-bit two's complement value.

questions.questionText: On the 8086, DX = 0001H, AX = FFFFH, CX = 0002H and BX = 0001H. What are DX and AX after ADD AX, BX / ADC DX, CX?
questions.explanation: ADD AX, BX: FFFFH + 0001H = 0000H with CF = 1. ADC DX, CX: 0001H + 0002H + CF = 0004H. The 32-bit sum is 0004 0000H (1FFFFH + 20001H = 40000H).

questions.questionText: What is in register B when this 8085 program halts (CY = 0 at the start)? MVI A, 0B5H / MVI B, 00H / MVI C, 08H / L: RAL / JNC SKIP / INR B / SKIP: DCR C / JNZ L / HLT
questions.explanation: Each of the 8 passes rotates one bit of the original A into CY, and B counts the 1s. B5H = 1011 0101 contains five 1s, so B = 05H. INR and DCR do not disturb CY between RAL and JNC.
